42.13: He understands no worldly and no spiritual existence,
42.14: he understands no good work and no sin,
42.15: he understands no heaven and no hell,
42.16: and even the account which is to be rendered by the soul he does not think of.'

43.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
43.2: thus: 'How is it possible to make Aûharmazd, the archangels, and the fragrant, well-pleasing heaven more fully for oneself?
43.3: And how is it possible to make Aharman, the wicked, and the demons confounded, and to escape from hell, the depreciated and dark?'
43.5: thus: 'To make Aûharmazd, the lord, and the archangels, and the fragrant, well-pleasing heaven for oneself, and Aharman, the wicked, and the. demons confounded, and to escape from hell, the dark and depreciated, are possible thus:
43.6: that is, when they make the spirit of wisdom a protection for the back (pûstîkpânakîh),
43.7: and wear the spirit of contentment on the body, like arms and armour and valour,
43.8: and make the spirit of truth a shield,
43.9: the spirit of thankfulness a club, (To) the spirit of complete mindfulness a bow,
43.11: and the spirit of liberality an arrow;
43.12: and they make the spirit of moderation like a spear,
43.13: the spirit of perseverance a gauntlet, and they put forth the spirit of destiny as a protection.
43.14: In this manner it is possible to come to heaven and the sight of the sacred beings, and to escape from Aharman, the wicked, and hell, the depreciated.'

44.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
44.2: thus: 'How are the sky and earth arranged?
44.3: How are the flow and arrangement of the water in the world?
44.5: Where is the demon of winter more predominant?
44.6: And which country is the more undisturbed?'
44.8: thus: 'The sky and earth and water, and whatever else is within them are egg-like (khâîyak-dîs), just as it were like the egg of a bird.
44.9: The sky is arranged above the earth, like an egg, by the handiwork of the creator Aûharmazd;
44.10: and the semblance of the earth, in the midst of the sky, is just like as it were the yolk amid the egg; [
44.11: and the water within the earth and sky is such as the water within the egg.]
44.12: 'And the flow of the water of every kind which is in the world is. from the region of Arzah
44.13: there where the sun comes up; and its downward surge (nîgun bâlisnŏ) is towards the region of Savah
44.14: where the sun goes down; and the surging on (âbâlisnŏ) of the water is into the sea Pûtîk,
44.15: and from the sea Pûtîk it goes back to the sea Varkash.
44.16: 'The abode and seat of the clouds are on Albûrz.
44.17: 'The demon of winter is more predominant in Aîrân-vêgô.
44.18: And it is declared by revelation,
44.19: that in Aîrân-vêgô there are "ten months winter and two months summer,"
44.20: and "even those" two months of warm weather "are cold as to water, cold as to earth, and cold as to plants." 21. And their adversity is the winter,
44.22: and the snakes therein are many,
44.23: while their other adversity is little.
44.24: 'It is declared that Aûharmazd created Aîrân-vêgô better than other places and districts.
44.25: And its goodness is this, that the life of the people is three hundred years,
44.26: and of the oxen and sheep one hundred and fifty years.
44.27: Their pain and sickness, also, are little;
44.29: they make no lamentation and weeping,
44.30: and the domination of the demon of greediness (A z) in their bodies is little.
44.31: When they eat one loaf among ten men, they are satisfied.
44.32: And in every forty years one child is born from one woman and one man.
44.33: Their law, also, is goodness, and their religion the primitive faith;
44.34: and when they die they are righteous.
44.35: Their spiritual chief (ratû), likewise, is Gôpaîtŏ, and their lord and king is Srôsh.'

45.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
45.2: thus: 'By what does Aharman most deceive and lead people to hell?
45.3: And from what is his pleasure most?
45.4: Where is the place he has a foundation?
45.5: Where, also, is his coming, together with the demons, most?
45.6: And from what is his food?'
45.8: thus: Aharman deceives people most by prosperity and adversity, the fiend of apostasy, scepticism, and covetousness.
45.9: His pleasure, also, is most from the discord of men.
45.10: And his food is from the impenitence and reticence of men.
45.11: He has a foundation in the malicious.
45.12: And his coming and going are most with the wrathful.'

46.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
46.2: thus: 'Which is the one oppression, as regards men, that Aharman considers as the more injurious and great?'
46.4: thus: Aharman, when he wrings life and wife and child and worldly happiness of every kind away from men, does not consider, as to this, that any injury whatever is inflicted by him upon that person;
46.5: but when he wrings away the soul of a single individual, and makes it utterly depraved, he then considers, as to this, that "an injury which is complete would thereby be inflicted by me," because this is done by him through his own depravity of wish and action.'

47.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
47.2: thus: 'What is that thing which is the most perfect of all wealth?
47.3: What is that which is predominant over everything whatever?
47.4: And what is that from which no one is able to escape?'
47.6: thus: 'It is wisdom which is better than the wealth of every kind which is in the world.
47.7: It is destiny which is predominant over every one and everything.
47.8: And it is Vâê the bad from whom no one is able to escape.'

48.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
48.2: thus: 'How is the dwelling of the understanding and intellect and seed of men in the body?'
48.4: thus: 'The place of the understanding and intellect and seed of men is in the brain of the head.
48.5: And when the brain of the head is sound, the understanding and intellect and seed are on the increase;
48.6: but when a person attains unto old age, the brain of the head remains only at a diminution.
48.7: And he who is an aged man, on account of the diminution of understanding and intellect, sees less and knows less of that which it is necessary to do with wisdom.
48.8: Wisdom, in the beginning, mingles with the marrow of the fingers of men's hands;
48.9: and, afterwards, its seat and abode and place are in the heart.
48.10: And its dwelling in the whole body becomes such as the shape of the foot in various shoes (mûgkakŏ). '

49.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
49.2: thus: 'As to these stars which are apparent in the sky, and their number is so great, what is then their duty and influence?
49.3: And how is the motion of the sun and moon and stars?'
49.5: thus: 'Of the stars which are in the sky the first star is Tîstar, which is said to be great and good, more valuable and more glorious.
49.6: And prosperity of every kind and the fertility of the world are in the path of Tîstar.
49.7: 'And the star of water germs is for the increase of the star of plant germs.
49.9: And the star of plant germs is for the increase of cattle germs.
49.11: And water, fire, plant, and cattle germs are created for the increase of man germs.
49.12: 'And the star Vanand is intrusted with the passes and gates of Albûrz;
49.13: so that the demons and witches and fiends may turn from those gates and passes,
49.14: that it may not be possible for them to cut off and break up the road and passage of the sun and moon and stars.
49.15: 'And the star Haptôk-ring, with 99,999 guardian spirits of the righteous, is intrusted with the gate and passage of hell,
49.16: for the keeping back of those 99,999 demons and fiends, witches and wizards, who are in opposition to the celestial sphere and constellations of the zodiac.
49.17: Its motion, also, is round about hell;
49.18: and its special business is this, as it were it holds the twelve signs of the zodiac by the hand, in their proper going and corning.
49.19: And those twelve constellations also proceed in like manner by the power and help of Haptôk-ring;
49.20: and every single constellation, when it comes in at Albûrz, provides support for Haptôk-ring,
49.22: 'The remaining unnumbered and innumerable constellations which are apparent are said to be the guardian spirits of the worldly existences.
49.23: Because, as to the creatures and creations of every kind, that the creator Aûharmazd created for the worldly existence, which are procreative and also which are developable (ârôdisnîk), for every single body there is apparent its own single guardian spirit of a like nature.
49.24: 'And the motion of the sun and moon is the special illumination of the world,
49.25: and the maturing of procreations and growths of all kinds.
49.26: And the correct keeping of the day, month, and year, summer and winter, spring and autumn, and other calculations and accounts of all kinds which men ought to obtain, perceive, and understand,
49.27: are more fully defined by means of the setting (nisîvakŏ) of the sun and moon.'

50.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
50.2: thus: 'Which is that opulent person who is to be considered as fortunate, and which is that one who is to be considered as evil-conditioned?'
50.4: thus: 'That one who has produced opulence by proper exertion is to be considered as fortunate; and that one who has produced it by dishonesty, as evil-conditioned.'

51.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
51.2: thus: 'Wherefore is it when there are instances when a lazy, ignorant, and bad man attains to eminence and great welfare,
51.3: and there are instances when a worthy, wise, and good man attains to grievous misery, perplexity, and indigence?'
51.5: thus: 'As to him who is a lazy, ignorant, and bad man, when his destiny becomes a helper, that laziness of his then becomes like unto diligence, that ignorance unto knowledge, and that vileness unto goodness.
51.6: And as to him who is a wise, worthy, and good man, when his destiny is an opponent, that wisdom of his then turns to stupidity and foolishness (alakîh), and that worthiness to ignorance;
51.7: and his knowledge, skill, and worthiness become manifestly secluded.'

52.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
52.2: thus: 'How is it necessary to perform the ceremonial of the sacred beings and the thanksgiving for the welfare which is owing to the sacred beings?
52.3: And how is the renunciation of sin to be performed for the preservation of the soul?'
52.5: thus: 'That ceremonial of the sacred beings is good which they perform in this pure, good religion of the Mazda-worshippers.
52.6: Its origin, also, is goodness and truth, and freedom from doubt in the sacred beings.
52.7: And for the little and the much that has come there has arisen thanksgiving unto the sacred beings; and one is to meditate upon the gratifications (shnûmakân) and prosperity which are owing to the, sacred beings and to keep grateful.
52.8: And even when perplexity and misery come on from Aharman and the demons, he is not to become doubtful as to the treasure of the sacred beings,
52.9: and not to diminish the thanksgiving unto the sacred beings.
52.10: And every disaster which springs up he is to give back to the violence of Aharman and the demons.
52.11: He is not to seek his own welfare and advantage through the injury of any one else;
52.12: and he becomes compassionate as regards the creatures of Aûharmazd.
52.13: In duty and good works he is diligent and striving;
52.14: and especially in the care of water and fire he is to persevere much.
52.15: And he is to be without doubt as to this, that, except happiness, the sacred beings do not then give anything whatever, as a modification of it, unto men; and Aharman and the demons, except misery, do not then give them any happiness.
52.16: 'For the existence of renunciation of sin the special thing is this, that one commits no sin voluntarily;
52.17: and if, through folly, or weakness and ignorance, a sin occurs, he is then in renunciation of sin before the high-priests and the good.
52.18: And after that, when he does not commit it, then that sin which is committed by him becomes thus a sweeping (êsvârakŏ) from his body;
52.19: just as the wind which is hasty and mighty, when it comes swift and strong, sweeps so over the plain that it carries away every single blade of grass (gîyyâkîkakŏ-1) and anything which is broken in that place.'

53.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
53.2: thus: 'How are the homage and glorifying of the sacred beings to be performed?'
53.4:
thus:
'Every day three times, standing opposite the sun and Mitrô, as they proceed together,
53.5: and the moon and fire of Vâhrâm, or the fire of fires, in like manner, morning, noon, and evening, homage and glorifying are performed,
53.7: And if a sin, or a deficiency (frôdmând-1), has occurred, especially as regards the angels of the spiritual and worldly existences, then and beasts of burden, oxen and sheep, dogs and the dog species, and other creatures and creations of Aûharmazd the lord,
53.8: one is to become sorrowful, penitent, and in renunciation of sin before the sun and Mitrô, the moon and the fire of Aûharmazd;
53.9: and, for the sake of atonement for the sin, good works are to be practised as much as is well possible.'

54.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
54.2: thus: 'Wherefore is it when an ignorant man—when they bring advancement to him—considers the learning and advancement of the wise and good mostly so, through greediness, that to teach it to him is difficult?'
54.4: thus: 'For this reason, because the ignorant man considers, in thought, his own ignorance as good as the sage does, in thought, his own knowledge.'

55.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
55.2: thus: 'Wherefore is he who is an ill-natured man no friend of the good, nor an untalented man of a talented one?'
55.4: thus: 'For this reason, because he who is an ill-talented man is at [all] times in fear of the talented,
55.5: lest "they should trouble us by their skill and talent, and, owing to that circumstance, shame may come upon us before the good and our opponents."
55.6: 'And the ill-natured are no friends of the good for this reason, because there is a time for their annihilation and destruction by the hands of the good.'

56.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
56.2: thus: 'Wherefore are these mountains and rivers made, which are in the world?'
56.4: thus: 'Of these mountains, which are in the world, there are some which are moderators of the wind, and there are some which are warders off;
56.5: there are some which are the place and vent, the resting-place and support of the rainy cloud;
56.6: and there are some which are smiters of Aharman and the demons, and maintainers and vivifiers of the creatures and creation of Aûharmazd, the lord.
56.7: 'And these rivers, which are in the world, the creator Aûharmazd has formed, from the borders of Albûrz, for providing the protection and for the vivification of his own creatures and creation.'

57.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
57.2: thus: 'Wherefore is it when the knowledge and sagacity of the spiritual and worldly existences, both united, are connected with thee?'
57.4: thus: 'For this reason, because, from the first, I, who am the innate wisdom, apart from the spiritual and worldly existences, have been with Aûharmazd.
57.5: And the creator Aûharmazd created (âfrîdŏ) the angels of the spiritual and worldly creations, and all the other creatures and creations through the power and mightiness, the wisdom and sagacity of innate wisdom; and I produce and he maintains and stimulates them.
57.6: And at the end of the renovation of the universe it is possible to cause the annihilation and destruction of Aharman and his miscreations more fully by the power of wisdom;
57.7: and Sôshâns, with Kaî-Khûsrôî, and those who the resurrection and future existence are able to act more fully, by means of the power and help of wisdom.
57.8: 'The knowledge and sagacity of the worldly existence, the learning and teaching in every profession, and all advancement of temporal beings are through wisdom:
57.9: The souls of the righteous, in escaping from hell and coming to heaven and the supreme heaven (garôdmân), arrive much better by means of the power and protection of wisdom.
57.10: And it is possible to seek the good living, pleasure, good repute, and every happiness of people in the worldly existence, through the power of wisdom.
57.11: 'And the maintenance of the seeds of men and beasts of burden, oxen and sheep, and also every other creature and creation of Aûharmazd, the lord, the seating of them in the womb, and making manifest what is their food in the womb, so that they shall not die from hunger and thirst, and the allotment and maturing of the limbs are effected more fully by means of the durability (dôrângarîh) and great potency which are in the force of wisdom.
57.12: 'The arrangement of the earth and the mingling of the water in the earth, the growth and increase of plants, colour of various kinds, and the scent, taste, and pleasantness of various things are allotted and produced more fully through wisdom.
57.13: And the arrangement of Albûrz around the world, the manifestation of the earth of the seven regions and the sky above the mountain of Albûrz, the motion of the sun and moon and twelve constellations, the six times of the season festivals (gâsanbâr). the five times devoted to the guardian spirits (fravardîkân), the heaven which is in the place of good thoughts, the place of good words, the place of good deeds, and the perfect supreme heaven (garôdmân) of all gloriousness, the path of the spirits and worldly existences, and the Kindvar bridge are produced and allotted through the power of wisdom.
57.14: 'The watery-looking cloud's seizing water from the sea, advancing in the atmosphere, and gradually breaking away, drop by drop, to the earth, and Aûharmazd's creatures’ thoroughly understanding the nature of heaven and hell, the compassion of Aûharmazd, the archangels, and other angels as regards their own creatures, and the devastation and destructiveness of Aharman and the demons as regards the creatures of Aûharmazd it is possible to comprehend through the more complete power of wisdom.
57.15: And the good religion of the Mazda-worshippers, the sayings and teaching of the spirits, and the demons’ demolishing the worldly body and making it imperceptible by the sight of men are apprehended more fully by means of the most perfect means of wisdom.
57.16: And even the struggle and warfare of Irân with foreigners (an-aîrân), and the smiting of Aharman and the demons it is possible to effect through the power of wisdom.
57.17: 'To occasion the sun's inspection of the hidden water also, below the earth, it is expedient to convey it for tillage and cultivation, and the advantage, comfort, and enjoyment of men and beasts of burden, oxen and sheep, through the power of wisdom.
57.18: The thorough understanding of the pain and sickness of men and beasts of burden, oxen, sheep, and other animals, and the bringing of medicine and remedies, health of body and comfort unto them are much more possible to effect by means of the power of wisdom.
57.19: 'And as to every man whose participation in wisdom is. much, his share of heaven is then much more.
57.20: Even as to Vistâsp, Zaratûst, Gâyômard, and those others whose share of heaven was much the more, it was on account of the much coming of wisdom unto them.
57.21: And as to Yim, Frêdûn, Kâî-Ûs, and those other rulers who obtained splendour (vargŏ) and mightiness (tagakîh) from the sacred beings just as the participation of Vistâsp and other rulers in the religion occurred —and their not attaining to the religion, and also as to the times when they have become ungrateful unto their own lord, it was on account of the little coming of wisdom unto them.
57.22: 'And Aharman, also, and the demons deceive that man more, and lead him to hell, who is poorer of wisdom and unsteadier in disposition.
57.23: And it is manifest, that, unto him who is virtuous in disposition, habit, and demeanour, praise is then due, owing to his maintenance of wisdom.
57.24: For it is declared, that Aharman shouted to Zaratûst thus: "If thou desist from this good religion of the Mazda-worshippers, then I will give thee a thousand years’ dominion of the worldly existence,
57.25: as was given to the Vadakân monarch Dahâk." 26. On account of complete wisdom, the virtuous disposition and demeanour of Zaratûst not having hearkened and not being deluded, he did not become deceived and longing through that temptation of the accursed evil one, the wicked.
57.28: thus: "I will shatter and cause to run (dûkânam), and will make downcast (nigûîsâr) for thee, the bodies of your demons and fiends, wizards and witches, through the Hôm and sacred twigs, and the good, true religion which the creator Aûharmazd has taught to me." 29. Aharman, when those words were heard by him, became confounded and stupefied, and rushed to hell, and remained confounded a long time.
57.30: 'This, too, is declared, that Aûharmazd, when Aharman, by agreement, had further operated with his (Aûharmazd's) creatures and creation of every kind, afterwards formed an assembly with the angels and archangels of every kind, and the welfare (âvâdîh) due to his own wisdom was mentioned and recounted by him.
57.31: 'This, too, is declared, that for the nine thousand years of renovation, until the resurrection and future existence, wisdom maintains and stimulates the creatures and creation of every kind.
57.32: 'And this, too, is declared, that, as to him who is an ignorant and bad-tempered man, when he attains even to much eminence, opulence, and authority, even then he is not fit to elevate into that welfare and authority.'

58.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
58.2: thus: Wherefore is it when one turns the ignorance and foolishness of an ignorant king back to knowledge and cleverness, on account of the sovereignty which is his;
58.3: and, as to a poor man, who is wise, one turns the knowledge and sagacity, which are his, back to foolishness and uselessness, on account of the poverty?'
58.5: thus: 'On account of the deceit and violence of the fiend of greediness
58.6: men utter more words as to the manliness of every one whose wealth and power are more, and recount his deeds and actions more fully;
58.7: but, in the eyes of the angels and archangels, a poor man who is innocent and wise is better and more precious than a king or opulent man who is ignorant.'

59.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
59.2: thus: 'What are the vices of priests?
59.3: What are the vices of warriors?
59.4: What are the vices of husbandmen?
59.5: And what are the vices of artizans?'
59.7: thus: 'The vices of priests are heresy, covetousness, negligence, trafficking (sûdakîh), attention to trifles, and unbelief in the religion.
59.8: 'The vices of warriors are oppression, violence, promise-breaking, unmercifulness (an-avôkhshâgâ-vandîh), ostentation (dakhshîh), haughtiness, and arrogance.
59.9: 'The vices of husbandmen are ignorance, enviousness, ill-will, and maliciousness.
59.10: 'And the vices of artizans are unbelief, want of thanksgiving, improper muttering of prayers, moroseness, and abusiveness.'

60.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
60.2: thus: 'Of mankind which are more conversant with good and evil?'
60.4: thus: 'Of mankind he whose sojourn and business are with the bad, and they provide him a name for good repute and goodness, is the man more conversant with good.
60.5: And he whose sojourn and business are with the good, and they provide him a name for disrepute, is the man more conversant with evil.
60.6: 'Because it is said, (7, 8) that whoever joins with the good brings good with him, and whoever joins with the bad brings evil—(9) just like the wind which, when it impinges on stench, is stench, (10) and when it impinges on perfume, is perfume,—(11) it is, therefore, notorious, (12) that he whose business is with the good receives good, (13) and he whose business is with the bad receives evil; (14) but, even then, both are to be considered as an experiment (aûzmâyisnŏ).'

61.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
61.2: thus: 'Which is the chief of men? Which is the chief of women?
61.3: Which is the chief of horses? Which is the chief of flying creatures?
61.4: [Which is the chief of oxen?] Which is the chief of wild animals? Which is the chief of grains?'
61.6: thus: 'The man who is wise, who is steadfast in the religion, who is well-praising, who is true-speaking is chief over his associates.
61.7: 'The woman who is young, who is properly disposed, who is faithful, who is respected, who is good-natured, who enlivens the house, whose modesty and awe are virtuous, a friend of her own father and elders, husband and guardian, handsome and replete with animation is chief over the women who are her own associates.
61.8: 'The ox which is glorious, which is tall-eared, which has a herd of cows is chief over oxen.
61.9: 'The Kîharâv is the chief of birds.
61.10: The horse which is swift is the chief of horses.
61.11: The hare is the chief of wild animals; and wheat is the chief of grains.'

62.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
62.3: Where is the enclosure formed by Yim constructed?
62.4: In what place lies the body of Sâhm?
62.5: Where is the abode of Srôsh?
62.6: In what place stands the three-legged ass?
62.7: Where is the Hôm grown, the preparer of the dead, with which they restore the dead and produce the future existence?
62.9: With what work is the Kar fish intrusted?
62.10: Where has the griffon bird a nest (âsîyân)?
62.11: In what place sits Kînâmrôs, and what is his work?'
62.13: thus: 'Kangdez is intrusted with the. eastern quarter, near to Satavâyês,
62.15: 'The enclosure formed by Yim is constructed in Aîrân-vêgô, below the earth.
62.16: And every species and seed of all the creatures and creations of Aûharmazd, the lord, whatever is better and more select of man and beast of burden, of cattle and flying creatures is brought thither.
62.17: And every forty years one child is born from one woman and one man who are of that place;
62.18: their life, too, is three hundred years,
62.19: and their pain and disturbance are little.
62.20: 'The body of Sâhm is in the plain of Pêsândas, near to Mount Dimâvand.
62.21: And on that plain, except corn and the eatable things they sow and reap and live upon, there is not so much as a single other tree, or shrub, or plant;
62.22: and its golden colour is mostly wormwood.
62.23: And the angels and archangels have appointed 99,999 guardian spirits of the righteous as a protection for the body of Sâhm,
62.24: so that the demons and fiends may not injure it.
62.25: 'The abode of Srôsh is mostly in Arzah, and afterwards also in Savah and the whole world.
62.26: 'The three-legged ass sits amid the sea Varkash;
62.27: and as to water of every kind that rains on dead matter, the menstrual discharge, and other bodily refuse, when it arrives at the three-legged ass, he makes every kind clean and purified, with watchfulness.
62.28: 'The Hôm, which is the preparer of the dead, is grown in the sea Varkash, in that which is the deepest place;
62.29: and 99,999 guardian spirits of the righteous are appointed as its protection.
62.30: The Kar fish, too, ever circles around it, and always keeps the frog and other noxious creatures away from it.
62.31: 'Gôpaîtôshah is in Aîrân-vêgô, within the region of Khvanîras.
62.32: From foot to mid-body he is an ox, and from mid-body to the top he is a man.
62.33: And at all times he sits on the sea-shore,
62.34: and always performs the ceremonial of the sacred beings, and pours holy-water into the sea.
62.35: On account of which, through the pouring of that holy-water, innumerable noxious creatures in the sea will die.
62.36: Because, if he does not specially perform that celebration of the ceremonial, and does not pour that holy-water into the sea—where those innumerable noxious creatures shall utterly perish —then, whenever the rain shall rain, the noxious creatures have to rain just like rain.
62.37: 'The nest of the griffon bird is on the tree. opposed to harm, the many-seeded.
62.38: Whenever he rises aloft a thousand twigs will shoot out from that tree,
62.39: and when he alights he breaks off the thousand twigs and bites the seed from them.
62.40: And the bird Kînâmrôs alights likewise in that vicinity;
62.41: and his work is this, that he collects those seeds which are bitten from the tree of many seeds, which is opposed to harm, and he scatters (pargandêd) them there where Tîstar seizes the water;
62.42: so that, while Tîstar shall seize the water, together with those seeds of all kinds, he shall rain them on the world with the rain.'

63.1: The sage asked the spirit of wisdom
63.2: thus: 'Which is that good work which is greater and better than [all ] good works, and no trouble (angînakŏ) whatever is necessary for its performance?'
63.4: thus: 'To be grateful in the world,
63.5: and to wish happiness for every one.
63.6:
This is greater and better than every good work, and no commotion (angînakŏ) whatever is necessary for its performance.'
Peace and prosperity.

1.1: In the name of Aûharmazd, the lord, the greatest and wise, [the all-ruling, all-knowing, and almighty,
1.2: who is a spirit even among spirits,
1.3: and from his self-existence, single in unity, was the creation of the faithful.
1.4: He also created, by his own unrivalled power, the seven supreme archangels,] all the angels of the spiritual and worldly existences,
1.5: and the seven worldly characteristics which are man, animals, fire, metal, earth, water, and plants.
1.6: And man was created by him, as a control of the creatures, for the advancement of his will.
1.7: From him likewise came at various times, through his own compassion, mercifulness to his own creatures, religion, and a natural desire of the knowledge of purity and contamination.
1.8: So, also, as to the intellect, understanding, wisdom, knowledge, consciousness, and guardian spirit—which are the appliances of the soul that are seeking information of these spiritual appliances, the five which are the sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch,
1.9: through the five worldly appliances, which are the eye, the ear, the nose, the mouth, and the rubbing surfaces of the whole body—
1.10: he likewise created man with the accompaniment of these appliances, for the management of the creatures.
1.11: He also created the religion of omniscience like an immense tree,
1.12: of which there are one stem, two branches, three boughs, four twigs, and five shoots.
1.13: And its one stem is agreement.
1.14: The two branches are performance and abstinence.
1.15: The three boughs are Humat, Hûkht, and Huvarst, which are good thoughts, good words, and good deeds.
1.16: The four twigs are the four classes of the religion, by whom the religion and world are prepared,
1.17: which are priesthood, warriorship, husbandry, and artisanship.
1.18: The five shoots are the five rulers whose scriptural names are the house-ruler, the village-ruler, the tribe-ruler, the province-ruler, and the supreme Zaratûst.
1.19: And the one chief of chiefs, who is the king of kings, is the ruler of the world.
1.20: Likewise, the work manifested by him in the world—which is man—is in the likeness of these four classes of the world.
1.21: As unto the head is priesthood,
1.24: and unto the foot is artisanship.
1.25: So, also, of the four capabilities (hunarân) that are in man—which are temper, ability, wisdom, and diligence—
1.26: unto temper (khîm) is priesthood, as the greatest duty of priests is the temper that they do not commit sin on account of shame and fear;
1.27: unto ability (hunar) is warriorship, that is, the most princely adornment of warriors is the ability which is expended, the manliness which is owing to self-possession (khvadîh);
1.28: unto husbandmen is the wisdom (khirad) which is strenuous performance of the tillage of the world, and continuance unto the renovation of the universe;
1.29: and unto artisans is the diligence (tukhshâkîh) which is the greatest advancement of their class.
1.30: This arrangement of every kind is upon one stem, truth and agreement, opposing the fiend and his appliances which are co-existent.
1.31: These, which are recounted by me, are of many kinds and many species, as many are religious and many believing at a period that all are mutually afflicting, co-existent destroyers and injurers, one as regards the other.
1.32: And with the mutual afflictiveness, destructiveness, and combativeness which are theirs, one towards the other, they afterwards also contend against the one truth co-operatively and with united strength.
1.33: The possession of truth is the one power of the faithful, through the singleness of truth.
1.34: The many kinds of falsehood, which must become confused and mutually afflicting to many, are, in the aggregate, from one source of deceitfulness.
1.35: As to that, this composition is provided by me, who am Mardân-farukh son of Aûharmazd-dâd, as I saw in the age much religiousness and much good consideration of sects (kêshân) of many species;
1.36: and I have been fervent-mindedly, at all times in my whole youthful career, an enquirer and investigator of the truth of them.
1.37: For the same reason I have wandered forth also to many realms and the seashore.
1.38: And of these compendious statements which, owing thereto, are an enquiry of those desiring the truth, and a collection and selection (vigîdanŏ) of it, for these memoranda, from the writings and memoranda of the ancient sages and high-priests of the just—and especially those of the glorified Âtûr-pâdîyâvand —the name Sikand-gûmânîk Vigâr is appointed by me.
1.39: As it is very suitable for explaining away the doubts of new learners about the thorough understanding of the truth, the blessedness and truth of the good religion, and the inward dignity of those free from strife.
1.40: And it is composed and arranged by me not for the wise and talented, but for preceptors (farhangîkân) and those newly qualified.
1.41: So that, while many become freer from doubt about the miraculousness and blessedness of the statements of the good religion and primitive faith,
1.42: I am still begging of distinguished sages,
1.43: that whoever wants to look, should not look to the religion of the particular speaker and composer, but to the greatness of the truth, blessedness, and definite statements of the ancient sages.
1.44: Because I, who am the composer, do not hold the station of teaching, but that of learning.
1.45: And it seemed to me, through liberal thought, a statement, from that knowledge of the religion, destined and important even for new learners.
1.46: Because he who distributes to the worthy, out of the little knowledge which is his, is more acceptable than he who knows much and the worthy are without benefit and without help from him.
1.48: that liberality is of three kinds, of thought, of word, and of deed.
1.49: Liberality of thought being that whose wishing of happiness for any others whatever, of a like disposition, is as much as for its own.
1.50: Liberality in word being that which teaches to the worthy something out of every virtuous knowledge and information which have come to it;
1.51: just as that which a certain sage said
1.52: thus: 'I desire that I may understand all information which is advantageous, and I will teach it to friends and acquire the result which is obtainable.'
1.53: And the liberality which is in deed being that which, out of any benefit whatever that has come to it, is a benefit to the worthy.
1.54: Again, it is a reminding of the good as to the preservation of the soul;
1.55: and for the same reason I have arranged that while the wise are kindly observant of me, through their own compassion, they may remember about the immortality of the soul.
1.56: Since it is said, that the eye of him who observes all good creatures with kind eyes is the eye of the sun;
1.57: because the sun is, indeed, an observer and beautifier with kind eyes for all creatures.

2.2: is about several questions that the ever-successful Mitrô-aîyyâr, son of Mahmâd, from Spâhân, asked with good intent and not in search of defects, and the answer thereto.
2.3: As to that which is asked thus: 'Why did Aharman hurry on to the light, and how was it possible to be so when he is not of a like nature with it, though we always see that whatever is not of a like nature abstains from a different nature as much as water does from fire?'
2.4: The answer is this, that the cause itself of the hurrying on of Aharman, which was to the light, was his different nature.
2.5: And on account of the desire of a destroyer, which was perpetually in his nature, he is a destroyer of different natures.
2.6: Being injured and injuring, however they occur, do not take place except from difference of nature and those of a different nature.
2.7: Because in those of a like nature there exist similarity of will and unanimity, one towards the other, not injuring and being injured.
2.8: And those of a different nature, on account of their opposing nature, are destroyers and injurers, one of the other, however they come together.
2.9: Those of a like nature, on account of unanimity and similarity of nature, are lively, efficient, and mutually helping, when they come together.
2.10: The disintegration and separation of like natures is the disunion of different natures.
2.11: Just as heat and cold which, on account of their opposing nature, are destroyers and injurers, resisting and disintegrating one another, through their perpetual nature.
2.12: Because every disintegration is owing to the laws (rastagân) of cold and dryness, heat and moisture,
2.13: and their destruction, injuring, and opposition of one another.
2.14: For the disintegration of bodies is owing to the perpetual struggling of heat and cold, dryness and moisture;
2.15: and owing to their struggling, one with the other, bodies are disintegrated and disabled.
2.16: Of water and fire, through their own nature, no injury whatever is manifest;
2.17: but the cold of their fraternization is mingled with the moisture of the water, and is an opponent of the heat of the fire;
2.18: and the dryness of their fraternization is mingled with the heat of the fire, and is counteractingly an injurer of the moisture of the water.

3.1: And as to that which is asked
3.2: thus: 'Why does not the creator Aûharmazd keep Aharman back from evil doing and evil seeking, when he is the mighty maker?
3.3: As I assert that no mighty maker is afterwards imperfect nor yet unresisting.'
3.5: that the evil deeds of Aharman are owing to the evil nature and evil will which are always his, as a fiend.
3.6: The omnipotence of the creator Aûharmazd is that which is over all that is possible to be, and is limited thereby.
3.7: That which is not possible to be is not stirred up by a capable or an incapable being.
3.8: Whoever says it is so is not within the limits of understanding the words.
3.9: Because, though he said that it is not possible to be, he says again that the sacred being is capable of it, and that has brought it out of the limits of what is not possible to be.
3.10: For then it is not the not-possible, but the possible to be.
3.11: As his capability is limited, so also is his will, thereby.
3.13: and the will of a sagacious being is all for that which is possible to be,
3.14: and his will does not pass on to that which is not possible,
3.15: because he wills all that which is possible and fit to be.
3.16: If I say that the creator Aûharmazd is able to keep Aharman back from the evil which is his perpetual nature,
3.17: it is possible to change that nature which is demoniacal into a divine one, and that which is divine into a demoniacal one;
3.18: and it is possible to make the dark light, and the light dark.
3.19: Of the changing of a nature by its own self those not understanding nature speak,
3.20: who are uninformed of the nature of the result in actions and propensities;
3.21: and they account the wolf and noxious creatures as a benefit.
3.22: Since the harm and evil which arise from mankind and cattle are not naturally their own, but are owing to the havoc, deceit, solicitation, and deluding of the fiend,
3.23: they are from the like vileness of other fiends who are such as the malice, wrath, and lust which are mingled with mankind.
3.24: Just as the swallowing of bitter medicine, which is mingled with poison, is not the accomplishment of happiness, but for the removal of the pain and sickness which are owing to an extraneous nature (barâ gôhar).
3.25: As of a statement which is true or false—
3.26: though it may be that, connected with a false statement, a righteous man is preserved from much harm, and is ruined by that which is true—
3.27: mostly that benefit is not from the false statement, but from the removal of the destruction and evil which are mingled with the vile,
3.28: and that harm is not from the true statement, but from the evil which is mingled with the vile.
3.29: Also, as regards that which happens when opponents have appeared in order to remove each one its own competitor,
3.30: every one is unrestricted in keeping away that which is its own opponent,
3.31: such as light and darkness, perfume and stench, good works and crime, erudition and ignorance.
3.32: That which is not unrestricted is the light to keep away stench, nor the perfume darkness;
3.33: but they have each separately appeared in order to keep away their own opponent.
3.34: As to that, too, which they say, that in the dark night a righteous man is preserved from the lion, wolves, dogs, and robbers,
3.35: while in the light day he becomes a captive in their hands,
3.36: it is not proper to consider that as a benefit owing to darkness, nor yet as an evil owing to light.
3.37: Because light is created for the removal of darkness, not for the keeping away of the lion, wolf, and noxious creatures. And there are many other things which are of this nature.
3.38: On account of tediousness this is collected merely as a summary; the virtue and understanding of you triumphant ones
3.39: are so much, that you may obtain more from revelation.

4.1: And as to that which is asked
4.2: thus: 'When I always see that all things ever arise from the celestial sphere and stars,
4.3: and who created this sphere, then it is like that which those of the Vîrôd religion say, that he created good and evil.
4.4: If Aharman created anything, how did he become able to create the effect of these marvellous things,
4.5: and why is it when they are stars by which assistance of virtue is always bestowed?
4.6: If Aûharmazd and Aharman created in conference, then that way it is manifest that Aûharmazd is an accomplice and confederate, with Aharman, in the harm and evil which ever arise from the celestial sphere.'
4.8: that the celestial sphere is the place of the divinities (baghân), who are the distributers of happiness, from which they always justly bestow their distribution of every happiness.
4.9: And the forms of the seven planets (star) are witches who rush below them, despoilers who are antagonistic distributers,
4.11: Through the creator Aûharmazd was the arrangement of these creatures and creation, methodically and sagaciously, and for the sake of the continuance of the renovation of the universe.
4.12: As the evil spirit was entangled in the sky, that fiend, with evil astuteness and with lying falsehood, encompassed and mingled with the light, together with the fiends of crimes of many kinds, who are those of a gloomy race, thinking thus: 'I will make these creatures and creation of Aûharmazd extinct, or I must make them for my own.'
4.13: Those luminaries, the highest of those of the good being, became aware, by means of omniscience, of the blemishing operation and the lies and falsehoods of the fiend,
4.14: and of this too, that is, of what extent was this power of his, by which this blemishing operation and work of ruin creep on,
4.15: so that, henceforth, there exists no power whatever for its restoration, which is free from the complete daubing of restraint, pain, and entanglement that is inside the sky.
4.16: It is they who are sagaciously mingled by him (the good being) with the substance of the luminaries, because that fiend encompassed and was entangled with his luminaries, therefore all his powers and resources are for the purpose of not allowing the fiends of crimes of many kinds their own performance of what is desirable for them each separately;
4.17: such as the fiendish venom of the noxious creatures which the four elements (zahakân), pertaining to Aûharmazd, [keep enveloped.
4.18:
For if this fiendish venom of the noxious creatures] does not remain entangled [with the four elements of the bodily formations pertaining to Aûharmazd]—which are water, fire, earth, and air—it is just as though they came to the sky and spiritual existence. 19.
And if they attained to spirituality and a disembodied existence, it would not be possible for those creatures of Aûharmazd to avoid and escape from that demoniacal venom of theirs.
4.20: It would be in the grasp (grôhê) and mingled with the breath (vâd) of mankind and the other creatures, and their restoration, support, increase, and growth would not be possible.
4.21: So they also keep those planets enveloped in light, because the fiendish venom of the noxious creatures is in the substance of those luminaries.
4.22: On account of that, too, the existence of somewhat of advantage is manifest from the serpent species, which are dissolving venom from the multitudes of other wild animals and noxious creatures.
4.23: So also from the planets; on account of the commingling of the inferior splendour of those luminaries, benefit is manifested by them.
4.24: A similitude of these planets and the benefit which they always bestow
4.25: is such as the brigands (gadûgân) and highwaymen who interrupt the path of traders in a caravan.
4.26: They abstract important things from many,
4.27: and do not grant and give them to the diligent and worthy, but to sinners, idlers, courtezans, paramours, and the unworthy.
4.28: Observe this, too, that this performance of good works which astrologers compute and state from those planets is for this reason,
4.29:
when they have not preferred the method of the divinities
(baghân) who are distributing welfare, and that, also, of the five constellations pertaining to Aûharmazd—which are the great one that is supreme and measurable, Haptôiring, created by Mazda, and the stars Vanand, Satavês, and Tîstar —as regards the brigands (gadûgân) and distributers of evil.
4.30: And those are the five planets that rush below them in the shape of stars, and they keep them enveloped in light, which are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.
4.31: Since the supreme constellation, the great one of the north-opposing
4.33: Haptôiring, created by Mazda, is opposing Jupiter,
4.34: Vanand, the smiter of noxious creatures, is opposing Mars,
4.35: the star Satavês is opposing Venus,
4.36: and the star Tîstar is opposing the planetary Mercury,
4.37: the welfare, which they say is from those brigands (gadûgân), is from those five constellations pertaining to Aûharmazd,
4.38: as they obtain the triumph of much power and little injury.
4.39: And for the sake of not leaving these five planets to their own wills, they are bound by the creator, Aûharmazd, each one by two threads (gîk) to the sun (Mihir) and moon.
4.40: And their forward motion and backward motion are owing to the same cause.
4.41: There are some whose length of thread is longer, such as Saturn and Jupiter,
4.42: and there are some of which it is shorter, such as Mercury and Venus.
4.43: Every time when they go to the end of the threads, they draw them back from behind,
4.44: and they do not allow them to proceed by their own wills,
4.45:
so that they may not injure the creatures.
4.6. And those two fiends that are greatly powerful, who are opponents of the planetary sun and moon, move below the splendour of those two luminaries.
4.47: Another—even that which is called the brigand (gadûg) of the stars, as regards the welfare that exists —is likewise confined below the splendour of the sun.
4.48: And when it gets far from control, it commits damage and harm on the constellation into which it springs, and on the quarter which is the particular concern of that constellation,
4.49: until it becomes again, a second time, bound and fettered to the sun.
4.50: The statement which they offer about it
4.51: is this, the conflict of the superior beings within the star station.
4.52: Out of the inferior of those are the conflicts of Tîstar and the demon Spenzagar,
4.53: of the fire Vâzist and the demon Avâush,
4.54: and of other good spirits with gloomy ones, for the formation of rain and allotment of welfare to the creatures.
4.55: Below them are mankind and cattle, noxious creatures and deadly ones, and other creatures that are good and bad.
4.56: Because propensities (gadasni) are mingled with mankind,
4.57: which are greed, lust, malice, wrath, and lethargy,
4.58: wisdom, temper, skill, knowledge, understanding, and intellect,
4.59: as the good influences and bad influences are called, which are the causes of good works and sin.
4.60: All this welfare of the creatures is specially owing to the creator of the creatures,
4.61: who is himself the healer and perfect ruler, the maintainer of protection, nourisher, and caretaker, preserving his own creatures.
4.62: And, for his own creatures, he has thoroughly created and taught the means of preservation from evil, and the appliances for abstaining from crime.
4.63: A semblance, too, of him is such as a wise orchard-owner and gardener who wishes to diminish the wild animals and birds which are mischievous and destructive for his orchard by spoiling the fruit of the trees.
4.64: And that wise gardener, effacing (padasâê) his own little trouble, for the sake of keeping those mischievous wild animals away from his own orchard, arranges the appliances which are necessary for the capture of those wild animals,
4.65: such as springes, traps, and snares for birds.
4.66: So that when a wild animal sees the snare, and wishes to proceed with suspicion of it, through unconsciousness of the springe and trap he is captured therein.
4.67: This is certain, that, when a wild animal falls into a trap, it is not a victory of the trap, but that of the arranger of the trap,
4.68: and through him the wild animal is captured in the trap.
4.69: The proprietor and orchard-owner, who is the arranger of the trap, is aware through sagacity that the wild animal is powerful, and to what extent and how long a time.
4.70: The power and strength of that wild animal, which are in its body, are exhausted and poured out by struggling, as much as it is able, in demolishing the trap and in endeavouring to destroy and spoil the springe.
4.71: And when, on account of imperfect strength, its power of struggling totters and is exhausted, that wise gardener then, by his own will and his own result of determination, wisely throws that wild animal out of the trap, with its existing nature and exhausted strength.
4.72: And he consigns his own trap and springe, rearranged and undamaged, back to the storehouse.
4.73: Even like him is the creator Aûharmazd, who is the preserver of creations and arranger of creatures, the disabler of the evil original evolution and protector of his own orchard from the injurer.
4.74: The mischievous wild animal, which is the spoiler of the orchard, is that accursed Aharman who is the hurrier and disturber of the creatures.
4.75: The good trap is the sky, in which the good creations are lodging,
4.76: and in which the evil spirit and his rudimentary miscreations are captured.
4.77: And pertaining to the springe and trap of the wild animal, who is mischievous owing to his own wilfulness, is the exhauster
4.78: time that, for the struggling of Aharman and his powers and resources, is for the long period
4.79: which, through the struggling of the wild animal in the springe and trap, is an exhaustion of its strength.
4.80: The sole creator of the creatures arranges a preservation again, which is the preparation of an eternal happy progress free from his adversary, which that wise orchard-owner does with his own trap and springe.
4.81: Then the scanty power and want of ability of that fiend for it, in his struggling for the luminaries, are manifest even from this.
4.82: When as with lying falsehood he thought thus: 'I will make this sky and earth and the creatures of Aûharmazd extinct, or I will turn them from their own nature and bring them to my own,'
4.83: even then, with all the power, desire of destruction, and perpetual struggling of the fiend, no slaughter whatever by the demons is free from effectual limits; it is this earth and sky, and these creatures,
4.84: that are propagating from few to many, as is manifest,
4.85: and innumerable persons are convinced of it.
4.86: For, if in this struggling any victory should have specially occurred, it would have been impossible to attain from few to many.
4.87: Moreover, if the births of the worldly existence are mostly manifest through the occurrence of death therein, even then it is seen that that death is not a complete dissolution of existence, but a necessity of going from place to place, from duty to duty.
4.88: For, as the existence of all these creations is derived from the four elements, it is manifest to the sight that those worldly bodies of theirs are to be mingled again with the four elements.
4.89: The spiritual parts, which are the rudimentary appliances of the life stimulating the body, are mingled with the soul—
4.90: on account of unity of nature they are not dispersed—
4.91: and the soul is accountable (amârhômand) for its own deeds.
4.92: Its treasurers, also, unto whom its good works and offences are intrusted, advance there for a contest.
4.93: When the treasurer of the good works is of greater strength, she preserves it, by her victory, from the hands of the accuser, and settles it for the great throne and the mutual delightfulness of the luminaries;
4.94: and it is assisted eternally in virtuous progress.
4.95: And when the treasurer of its offences is of greater strength, it is dragged, through her victory, away from the hands of the helper,
4.96: and is delivered up to the place of thirst and hunger and the agonizing abode of disease.
4.97: And, even there, those feeble good works, which were practised by it in the worldly existence, are not useless to it;
4.98: for, owing to this same reason, that hunger and thirst and punishment are inflicted on it proportionately to the sin, and not lawlessly,
4.99: because there is a watcher of the infliction of its punishment.
4.100: And, ultimately, the compassionate creator, who is the forgiver of the creatures, does not leave any good creature captive in the hands of the enemy.
4.101: But, one day, he saves even those who are sinful, and those of the righteous through atonement for sin, by the hands of the purifiers, and makes them proceed on the happy course which is eternal.
4.102: The conclusion is this, that the creator is the healer and perfect ruler, the maintainer and nourisher, protecting and preserving the creatures; not a producer of the disease, a causer of the pain, and an inflicter of the punishment of his own creatures.
4.103: And it is more explicitly written below, with the arrangement of the two original evolutions, among the assertors of the non-existence of a sacred being, and the contemplators of unity.
4.104: As ordered and requested by you it is provided (padarâst); do you direct and observe it with kind regards.
4.105: Because, as written above by us, I do not hold the station of teaching, but really that of learning.
4.106: Even this teaching of doctrines is that which was obtained by me, through the religion of wisdom, from the writing (nipîk) of Âtûr-pâdîyâvand, and is here indicated.
4.107: And his teachings are in the Dînkard manuscript (nipîk), which the supremely learned Âtûr-frôbag, son of Farukh-zâd, who was the leader of those of the good religion, explained out of his knowledge of the religion, and which consists of a thousand subjects.
4.108: Of that, too, which is asked by you about unlimitedness and limitation, I have written below, through the will of the sacred beings.

5.1: Another subject, among the assertors of the non-existence of a sacred being, is about the existence of the sacred being and his competitor.
5.2: Of the knowledge approvable by wisdom and the statements of the limits of evidence, about the existence of the sacred being and his competitor,
5.3: this is a summary:—One knows it should be enjoined, that the supreme first knowledge, most suitable for the well-discerning, is comprehending the sacred being.
5.4: He, of whom this knowledge is not the leader of knowledge, is unaided by other knowledge.
5.5: Comprehending the sacred being is possible through undecayed understanding, fervent intellect, and decisive wisdom.
5.6: Since comprehending the sacred being is not, thus far, more than that one knows that a sacred being exists,
5.7: because whoever is acquainted with the existence of a certain thing, and is unaware of its nature, is thinking thus, that that thing is good or bad, erudite or ignorant, antidote or poison, cold and frozen or hot and scorching, dry and withering or damp,
5.8: and, when unaware of its nature, his only knowledge of it is then useless—
5.9: for it is possible to cause the commendation and condemnation of any person or thing, not through its existence but through its nature—
5.10: therefore one knows this should be also enjoined, that a knowledge of anything is acquired in three modes:—
5.11: by knowing what is inevitable, or by knowing what is analogous, or by what is possible and fit to exist.
5.12: Inevitable knowledge is such as once one is one, and twice two are four.
5.13: For within the bounds of the really inevitable it is not possible to say,
5.14: that there was or will be a time, or a place, where twice two are said to be five or three.
5.15: Knowledge by analogy is that which announces, from anything manifest, something which is not manifest,
5.16: and brings, out of anything visible, something invisible, in the likeness of a hand put up, for the household service of the perception of wisdom,
5.17: through complete similarity, resemblance, or partial resemblance.
5.18: Complete similarity is such as that of a man of Pârs to a man of another district.
5.19: Resemblance is such as that of cheese to the white of an egg.
5.20: And partial resemblance is such as that of cheese to chalk,
5.21: since this is about the limit of partial resemblance, because cheese is like unto chalk only in whiteness,
5.22: but to the white of an egg in whiteness and also as food.
5.23: And there is also that which is called more resembling than resemblance, and more partially resembling than partial resemblance.
5.24: That which is more than complete similarity is not spoken about,
5.25: because completion does not become more complete.
5.26: By this mode it is set forth a second time at more length.
5.27: To demonstrate an invisible from a visible thing is such as from a thing made and maintained, which is not domestically serving the maker and maintainer,
5.28: and from a thing written, whose writer is not declared,
5.29: are manifest a maker of that which is made, a maintainer of that which is maintained, and a writer of that which is written, who are inevitable,
5.30: because that which is not manifest and is invisible is demonstrated by the thing which is manifest and visible.
5.31: Information of that which is within the possible and fit to exist is credible,
5.32: such as what one states thus: 'I saw a man by whom a lion, or a lion by whom a man, was slain outright.'
5.33: And this, being that which is within the limits of the possible and fit to exist, may be a lie.
5.34: But when a man announces that intelligence, who is renowned for truth and tested in judgment, it is within the limits of truth and reality.
5.35: If a man announces it, who is disgraced by falsehood and tested in misjudgment, it is within the limits of falsehood and unreality.
5.36: Another mode, outside of these and within the limits of the inevitable, is by knowing what has not occurred and is not possible;
5.37: such as what one states thus: 'It is possible to bring the world, in secrecy, into the inside of an egg,'
5.38: or 'it is possible for an elephant to pass into an eye of a needle,'
5.39: in such a manner as though one of them really becomes no greater and no less,
5.40: or its substance is something which is not a rudiment.
5.41: A struggle which should not be limited,
5.42: an existing thing which is not temporary and localised,
5.43: or is localised and not limited,
5.44: the working of a vain miracle,
5.45: and other things of this description of speaking and imagining are faulty and false and not possible.
5.46: Then the knowledge of the existence of him who is the exalted sacred being, apart from tangibility of nature and other evidence, is through the inevitable and analogy,
5.47: as much visible before the sight of wisdom as from the prosperity, formation, and organization which are, according to different statements of many kinds, the formation of the things of the world and mankind whose particles, and the appliances which are owing thereto, are such as the elements of the body and life, from which they are prepared and formed,
5.48: which are fire, water, air, and earth,
5.49: that are, each separately, a stimulus so qualified and ennobled for their own operations,
5.50: that the operation of fire, through its own quality (kîharîh) and nobility (vâspûharakânîh), is such that the operations of water, air, and earth are not to stimulate unrestricted (atang) by it.
5.51: Thus, also, the operation of water, through its own quality, is such that the operations of air, fire, and earth are not unrestricted by it.
5.52: So, also, of air, the operations of fire, water, and earth are not unrestricted by it.
5.53: So, also, of earth, the operations of these others are to stimulate not unrestricted by it.
5.54: But each separately is for its own operation, just as they are ennobled and qualified
5.55: by him who is, sagaciously and methodically, a qualifier, a constructor, and an ennobler.
5.56: And the organization is constructed, prepared, qualified, and ennobled as is suitable for those operations.
5.57: So, also, as to mankind and the other creatures, who are the germinating of these elements,
5.58: whose organization of bone, fat, sinew, veins, and skin, each separately
5.59: without sympathy, one for the other, is visible altogether.
5.60: Thus, too, are the nobility and qualification of the internal organs,
5.61: such as the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys, gall-bladder, and other appliances, for every one of which a function of its own is manifest.
5.62: They are qualified and ennobled for their defence by those functions which are their own.
5.63: So, also, is the qualification of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, mouth, teeth, hand, foot, and other external appliances, whose own functions are each separate.
5.64: And it is visibly manifest therein; inasmuch as, when one of these organs is disabled, any one of the rest is not suitable for the work of that other one, for which it is not qualified.
5.65: And when only the construction of one of the organs of the body is examined into—that is, how it is—it is wonderfully sagaciously constructed.
5.66: Such as the eye, which is of many natures of different names and different purposes,
5.67: as the eyelash, the eyelid, the white, the eyeball (khâyak), the iris (sâyak), and the pupil (têdak),
5.68: in such way that the white is fat,
5.69: the iris is water which has so stood in the prison of fat that the turning of the eye, from side to side, occurs through it,
5.70: and the pupil, itself the sight, is like a view into the water.
5.71: The iris stands in the prison of white, like the standing of water in a prison of fat;
5.72: and the pupil is within the iris, like the view of a thing within clear water,
5.73: or the form of a column in a shining mirror.
5.74: And the arrangement of the white in the orbit is for the reason that the dust whirling from the atmosphere, when it arrives at the eye, shall not be concealed in it,
5.75: but shall turn to the lid (gumb) of the eye,
5.76: and shall not injure the sight of the eye.
5.77: Just as the construction of the tube (rag) of the ear is undilated (afâhal), for the reason
5.78: that whirls of dust and winged noxious creatures shall not rightly enter therein.
5.79: And the moisture of oneself, the secretion of the ear, and the venom of noxious creatures are manifestly as useful.
5.80: When the appliances of life and soul are observed—
5.81: such as the smell, hearing; sight, taste, and touch which are causing the intelligence of living beings,
5.82: as also the wisdom of every pontiff (rad), which is pronounced decisive,
5.84: the intellect which is a seeker and transmitter,
5.85: the understanding which is a treasurer and defender,
5.86: the consciousness which is itself the sight of the soul,
5.87: the guardian spirit (fravash) which is itself the nature that is a maintainer of the body,
5.88: the spiritual life (ahû) which is pure,
5.89: and the other spiritual existences that are maintaining the body, which are each separately qualified, in that manner, for their operation and duty—
5.90:
they are perfect in their own operation, as to duty such as they are ennobled and qualified for. 91. As to that for which they are not qualified, they are not suitable.
92. The two arguments which are each separate in the Dînkard manuscript, as the supremely learned one has explained them out of his knowledge of the religion, are here set forth at length. 93. He whose wish is to fully understand the wonderfulness of the Mazda-worshipping religion and the statements of the primitive faith, (94) examines into it in a manuscript of that character, (95) and shall understand more fully the wonderfulness and truth of the religion.

6.1: As to another delusion of those asserting the non-existence of a sacred being—
6.3: that they are ordained free from religious trouble (alag) and the toil of practising good works,
6.4: and the unlimited twaddle (drâyisn) they abundantly chatter,
6.5: you should observe this:—6. That they account this world, with the much change and adjustment of description of its members and appliances, their antagonism to one another, and their confusion with one another, as an original evolution of boundless time.
6.7: And this, too, that there is no reward of good works, no punishment of sin, no heaven and hell, and no stimulator of good works and crime.
6.8: Besides this, that things are only worldly, and there is no spirit.
6.9: As I have written and shown above —
6.10: that to be made without a maker, and decided without a decider, is as impossible as to prepare what is written without a writer, or a house without a mortar-mixer (râz) and building (dêsâk)—
6.11: things made, of all kinds, cannot arise without making.
6.12: And this worldly existence is owing to the mingling of competing powers.
6.13: So its numerous possessions are so constructed, selected, and made of diverse races (kîharân), diverse colours, diverse scents, diverse characteristics, and diverse species as I have stated above about the body,
6.14: that it is constructed and made out of many things, such as bone, fat, sinew, veins, skin, blood, breath, hair, fundament, hand, foot, head, belly, and other members, internal and external,
6.15: in two series of things of many kinds, of which to be never made by means of the diverse nature of diverse powers,
6.16: or to arise without a maker, the impossibility is certain.
6.17: And in like manner of the other creatures, plants and trees, water and fire, earth and air, their stimulus, too, which is not themselves, is to their own duty; and they are not stimulators,
6.18: but there is a stimulator, a building (dêsâk), and a making for them.
6.19: And the usage (vâzâr) which is changing and urging them, from stimulus to stimulus, from statement to statement, and from time to time, is not according to the will and requirement of those made, but according to those that are stimulating and making.
6.20: Even so, indicative of the rotation of the years, months, days, and hours, is the revolution of the celestial sphere and stars which are settled (pasâkhtak), and of the sun and moon which are adjusted (nîvârdak), a well-horsed progress and conspicuous revolution.
6.21: This, too, is an indication that the movements of every appearance (kîharîh) are owing to an exhibitor, by whom the movement of that appearance is exhibited.
6.22: Owing to other differences and different management in the worldly existence
6.23: it is possible to know, from the worldly existence at various times and various periods, that this worldly existence is not without a manager.
6.24: Or that its manager is not a sacred being, who is learned, acting reasonably, of unlimited power, and illumining the sky, is also that which is visible when the development, decay, and death of the world are such, that the nature alike of mankind and animals, and alike of races and trees, is to come from youth to old age, and from old age to death.
6.25: No one whatever is seen that has come from old age back to youth, or from death back to life, and it is not possible to say so.
6.26: Nor yet is it proper to think, say, or believe this,
6.27: that there is no recompense of good works and punishment of crime,
6.28: nor even an appearance of an attainable creator of all the creatures, and of the daubing of a destroyer.
6.29: Moreover, as to this latter, that is precious to those who are more friends of penury than of the comfort of ill-famed vileness—
6.30: because they produce their happiness thereby, and are grateful,
6.31: and when they see distress they become suppliants
6.32: even from this destiny and dispensation which cannot become spiritual except by the spirits—
6.33: even so, in the appearance of every one of the hungry,
6.34: and in every one hurrying and straitened, who is imploring favours, is a manifestation of the maintenance of a hope for a supreme inspection over mankind, and, indeed, over wild animals, birds, and quadrupeds.
6.35: As to this, too, which they call sophistical.
6.36: that there is no assurance of even one of these things,
6.38: for whoever says that honey is bitter and honey is sweet, is right in both,
6.39: since it is bitter to those abounding in bile, and sweet to others;
6.40: also bread is pleasant and bread is unpleasant are both true,
6.41: since it is pleasant to the hungry, and unpleasant to the surfeited;
6.42: and many other statements of this description—
6.43: that which should be said in reply to their twaddle is summarily
6.44: such as the wise have told them
6.45:
thus:—'Even this statement of you sophists, about the jaundiced nature of everything, is alike jaundiced, and there is no truth in it.'
46. Many other things are said among them;
6.47: and this that is indicated by us is the predominant information for you victors,
6.48: so that you may obtain more from revelation.

7.1: Another subject is about the existence of a competitor of a different nature, as shown above,
7.2: that, from the constructing, qualifying, and ennobling of things so sagaciously, and even from the circumstances of an unimproving (akârîk) hand put upon the concentrated light, it is manifest that its maker, constructor, concentrator, and qualifier is sagacious.
7.3: Also his constructing sagaciously is manifest, from each separately, through the qualifying and ennobling of his own works severally.
7.4: And his working sagaciously is an indicator that his work is purposed and caused,
7.5: because every one of the works of the sagacious ought to be purposed and caused.
7.6: The purpose and cause of a work arise first, the work itself afterwards.
7.7: From the many kinds of his work it is manifest that his work is willed and requisite.
7.8: For there are two modes of doing a work,
7.9: either the willed is of the many kinds which are his will, (to) or the quality is of one kind which is as it is qualified;
7.11: so from the many kinds of work of the creator it is manifest that his work is willed and requisite.
7.12: And his will is owing to a necessity of different limit,
7.13: because his will was a requisite for the power of the original evolution.
7.14: The purpose and cause of a work are before the necessity,
7.15: because while the purpose of the necessity of a work does not occur, the necessity does not exist.
7.16: The purpose of a work arises from the cause, towards which the necessity of that work instigates.
7.17: The necessity and willing of a thing which is caused exist;
7.18: and a cause of the necessity of a thing owing to its own self is not well suited,
7.19: because the cause arises from progression,
7.20: concerning which an indicator is the purposed work that is sagacious.
7.21: The purpose is owing to a cause, the cause is owing to promptitude (aûstâv), the promptitude is owing to an exception (barâ), the exception is owing to an injurer, and the injury is owing to an opponent, without further words.
7.22: I have also shown, on this subject, through inevitable knowledge and through analogy, the making and qualification of the world and its circumstances and appliances.
7.23: From the making and qualification of the world is manifested a maker and qualifier;
7.24: and [through the purposely-made work of the sagacious creator,
7.25: owing to] the purposely-made work, is manifested the existence of an injurer from without.

8.1: Again, about the existence of a competing and different original evolution, there are these
8.2: that are manifest from the good and evil which are in the world,
8.3: and the particulars of its good maker which are self-limited.
8.11: and other co-existing factors whose certain existence is visible in every district and land, and every age.
8.12: So that no district or land whatever is discovered, nor yet any age has existed or shall exist,
8.13: wherein these good and bad terms and particulars have not existed or do not exist.
8.14: And it is not possible to say, as to any place or age, that good and evil are changeable in themselves by their own nature.
8.15: So, moreover, of the other co-existences whose difference is not through different duty, through different species, or through different quality—
8.16: as the difference of those of a like nature among one another, such as male and female,
8.17: of the varieties of scents and flavours, and of the sun and moon and stars, whose difference is not through different nature, but through different duty, through different qualification, and through different construction, which are such as are attainable for various duties—
8.18: the good and evil, light and dark, and other different natures are then their distinction not through different duty, but through different nature,
8.19: the incompatible quality and the injuriousness which are manifest in them, one towards the other.
8.20: Therefore, when good is there, the non-existence of evil is unquestionable;
8.21: when light has come, darkness is removed.
8.22: Even so of the other co-existences whose incompatibility and injuriousness together are owing to the cause of difference of nature,
8.23: because, in the worldly existence, there is a manifestation of the competing nature and injuriousness of the things, one towards the other.
8.24: The worldly existence is the fruit of the spiritual, and the spiritual is its root,
8.25: because fruit is obtained through a root.
8.26: In like manner the giver of the evidence arisen among the intelligent is clear.
8.27: Of the worldly existence being the fruit, and the spiritual being the root, the evidence is this,
8.28: when the progress (madanŏ) of every visible and tangible thing from imperceptibility to perceptibility is explicitly manifest.
8.29: Because the arising of mankind and other creatures, who are visible and tangible, from a spiritual existence which is invisible and intangible is known,
8.30: as much as the mirrored length and breadth of the body being an emanation of itself.
8.31: And the perceptibility of the body of man and other creatures was imperceptible and invisible in the semen which is derived from their fathers;
8.32: the semen itself, too, came into perceptibility, visibility, and tangibility in the skin of the fathers.
8.33: It is now possible to know inevitably that this worldly existence, which is visible and tangible, is produced and has arisen from a spiritual existence which is invisible and intangible.
8.34: In like manner the lapsing (yehevûntanŏ) from visibility and tangibility into invisibility and intangibility, which are themselves a spiritual state, is unquestionable.
8.35: When these are seen by us, in the worldly existence, the competing nature, formation, and injuriousness of one towards the other, even as to the property of the spiritual existence,
8.36: which is the root of the worldly one;
8.37: and, in like manner, there is no doubt of the existence of its fruit of worldly possessions;
8.38: this is that which is manifest as regards a competing nature.
8.39: Then its purpose and cause were indicated by me above, which are the sagaciously working of the creator,
8.40: who created the creature which is an indicator of the existence of an opponent.
8.41: For it is known that work due to workers is of two kinds, designed or qualified.
8.42: That which is designed is of three kinds.
8.43: Two are due to the wise and sagacious;
8.44: either through seeking for their own working of advantage and benefit,
8.45: or through removing and keeping away the harm and evil which are from without.
8.46: And one is due to the ignorant and unwise,
8.47: done defectively and without a purpose.
8.48: From the wise and sagacious, work ought not to arise without a purpose and without a cause.
8.49: As the sagacious creator, who is all-knowing, perfectly capable, and fully complete in his own self, has sought that which is not a necessity for any advantage and aggrandizement of his from without,
8.50: it is, therefore, necessary to understand that the purpose and causes of his works are of that one kind,
8.51: to remove and keep away the harm which is due to his opponent and the injurer who may arise from without, which is itself the purpose and cause of the creation of the creatures.
8.52: Also this, that that sagacious creator is good-willed,
8.53: and his will is all goodness.
8.54: The creatures were also created by him predominantly of his own will.
8.55: And the completely-stirring desire of him who is good-willed and sagacious is to subdue evil and make it extinct,
8.56: for while evil is not subdued the will of him who is good-willed is not fulfilled.
8.57: And this, that the goodness of that sagacious creator is manifest from creativeness, cherishing, and protection, and from commanding and teaching the means of putting away the path of evil and causing forbearance from crime;
8.58: also from the qualities and powers of the body in pain and sickness from without.
8.59: And, as a cause of the body,
