8.60: to remove and keep away the opponent who comes to the body, and to be the maintenance, the cause of maturity, and the cause of growth of animals and sprouting plants, through the power of maintaining and cherishing their qualities, there is a co-operator who is scripturally called the Fravash.
8.61: And through those four powers that are accumulative, which are the powers of attracting, seizing, digesting, and extracting—
8.62: and which, owing to the creator's sagacity of every kind, are co-operators with proportionate power for keeping away the pain and sickness of various kinds which are owing to the opponent, who is working defectively and desirous of evil—
8.63: and through others that are of like strength and auxiliary, the good will of the creator is manifest.
8.64: Of this, too, that this one is no creator of the pain and death which are dissipaters of the body, who is good-willed and a maintainer and cherisher of the body,
8.65: the evidence is even from this, when the sagacious creator is not a sufferer from sorrow (apakhshadâr) and performing penitence,
8.66: and is no dissipater and disabler of his own achievements,
8.67: because he is sagacious and all-knowing.
8.68: As to this other and the sorrow and penitence of the kind which is owing to his own work, it is fitting to speak about him as of deficient knowledge, incomplete wisdom, and inconclusive understanding.
8.69: As work does not arise from the wise and sagacious without a purpose and without a cause,
8.70: in like manner work from the unwise and ignorant and those of inconclusive understanding is all defective, without a purpose, and without a cause.
8.71: And that sagacious one is a contriver, working sagaciously and methodically, for keeping away that defective work and inconclusive understanding from his own creatures.
8.72: He who is working defectively produced distorted and entangled scriptures among the creatures;
8.73: because this is known, that it is not possible so to keep away and cramp him who is a moving and living nature in a boundless void, and to become without risk of injury.
8.74: But, though he does not become entangled, fenced in, and captive,
8.75: he is spreading anguish into the entanglement and captivity, and it is a means of grievous punishment.
8.76: Only while a complete wiping away of the anguish due to him, and complete information as to his own ignorant activity do not arise, he has meditated with lying falsehood on that which is connected therewith.
8.77: And the complete capability of the almighty creator is the wiping away of the anguish.
8.78: Owing to the complete wiping away of anguish, through the almightiness of the sagacious creator, he casts him back impotent into the boundless void.
8.79: And the good creatures thereby become fearless, immortal, and undistressed
8.80: through the completely methodical sagacity and discernment of means of that omniscient creator of good beings.
8.81: From observation of possessions the difference of things is manifest.
8.82: And the difference is of two kinds, as mentioned above.
8.83: One is difference of operation, and the other is difference of nature.
8.84: Difference of operation is owing to mutual assistance and united strength,
8.85: and difference of nature is owing to want of an adapter and to opposition.
8.86: And not in a single place is a permanence of possessions manifest.
8.87: If one of anything shall exist and one does not exist, its name shall exist,
8.88: for the sake of recognising things, one from the other, and preserving the name.
8.89: The bad, by separation from the good existence, is originally evolved in such a manner that the one is really no cause of the other.
8.90: Because each one is existent (aît-hômand) through its own self,
8.91: owing to the perpetual injury and antagonism which are manifestly theirs, one towards the other.
8.92: If any one shall say that, as the competing formations of the competitors are numerous—
8.93: such as good and evil, dark and light, perfume and stench, life and death, sickness and health, pleasure and vexation—
8.94: there ought to be many other such original evolutions, many in number and of many species;
8.95: then they may give this reply,
8.96: that, even when there are many names and many species of competitors, still then all are within the compass of two names.
8.97: And these two names are their including-source, which are good and evil.
8.98: Their different names and different species are tokens of these two sources.
8.99: There is nothing whatever that is not in the compass of these two names.
8.100: There has not been and will not be anything which is not good or evil, or a mixture of both.
8.101: On which account it is explicitly manifest that the original evolutions are two, and not more;
8.102: and also this, that it is not possible for good to arise from evil, and evil from good.
8.103: From this, too, it is possible to understand,
8.104: that it is not possible for complete evil to arise from that thing which is filled with goodness.
8.105: If it be possible, then it is not full;
8.106: because any one thing, when said to be full, is no place for anything else;
8.107: and when there is no place for anything else, other things are not improved by it.
8.108: If the sacred being be perfect in goodness and wisdom, the folly and evil of any one are known not to arise from him.
8.109: If it be possible for them to arise from him, then he is not perfect.
8.110: If he be not perfect, it is not proper to glorify him for the sacredness of complete goodness.
8.111: If good and evil have crept on from the sacred being, he is imperfect in goodness.
8.112: If he be imperfect in goodness, he is imperfect in good information.
8.113: Ifhe be imperfect in good information, so also he is imperfect in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, intellect, and other appliances of sagacity.
8.114: If he be imperfect in wisdom, understanding, intellect, and knowledge, he is imperfect in health.
8.115: If he be imperfect in health, he is apt to become sick.
8.116: If he be apt to become sick, he is imperfect in life.
8.117: If any one shall speak thus: 'I always see that from one nature, such as that of mankind, alike good and alike evil have always crept on, through actions owing to them,'
8.118: that is for this reason, because mankind are not perfect even in one thing.
8.119: And on account of imperfection in goodness, evil has crept on from them;
8.120: and also on account of imperfection, even in health, they become sick.
8.121: For the same reason they die,
8.122: because the cause of death is the struggling of two competing propensities within one nature.
8.123: There where two competing propensities exist within one nature, the occurrence of sickness and death is known.
8.124: If any one shall say that there are good and evil actions which, until they are done, do not exist,
8.125: then they may give this reply,
8.126: that the occurrence of an action apart from doing is as impossible as any propensity apart from a nature; and, as to the nature,
8.127: its continuance and arrangement are then known thereby not to occur through its own self.
8.128: For when a man indulges in wrath, Vohûman is far from there;
8.129: and when Vohûman holds the position, wrath is not there.
8.130: When a man tells a lie, truth is far from there;
8.131: and when he speaks true, falsehood has no position there, and that man is called truthful.
8.132: So also when sickness has come, health is not there;
8.133: and when health has come, sickness has gone.
8.134: Just as a substance which is not moving can exist,
8.135: but movement, except in a substance, cannot exist.
8.136: About this chapter, too, collected as a summary,
8.137: do you reverently and discreetly observe and instruct thereon.

9.1: Other information about the existence of the competitor, similarly testified by the Dînkard manuscript (nipîk), is here well noted for you.
9.2: For both this which is written above and that which is written here are all grown from the seed which the glorified Âtûr-pâdîyâvand sowed,
9.3: and from the original thanksgiving (spâs) of the supremely learned Âtûr-frôbag, son of Farukh-zâd, himself.
9.4: The fourth subject, which is from the Dînkard, is about the existence of an opponent of the creatures and of an opponent earlier than the creatures, and is from the exposition of the good religion.
9.5: That is, a knowledge of the existence of an opponent of the creatures is obtainable from the innermost recesses of the body of man even to the outermost objects of which sight is susceptible,
9.6: and beyond those, within the certain limits of analogy.
9.7: The innermost recesses of man are the innermost of life,
9.8: and are seen through complete observation, within the same limits.
9.9: This is, as ignorance is to erudition,
9.12: other defects of the capabilities which are the source of erudition, good disposition, and truth are the opponent,
9.13: and the cause of the wickedness of the soul.
9.14: Again, these irregularities of the rules of arrangement of the body, within the compass of the body, are the opponent, and the cause of the disintegration of the body.
9.15: Again, as to these among the emanations, cold is the opponent of heat, dryness is of moisture, and the other doers of mischief are opponents of the operations of existence.
9.16: Within time darkness is the opponent of light, stench of perfume, ugliness of handsomeness, unsavouriness of savouriness, poison of its antidote, noxious creatures and the wolf of the well-yielding cattle, and the vile felon (mar) of the good man.
9.17: Beyond time the brigand planets (gadûgân) are the opponents of the work of the divine bestowers.
9.18: Beyond the knowledge obtainable of all these champions susceptible to sight, are those who are within the limits of analogy and the certain information of multitudes, the demons who are the opponents of the sacred beings.
9.19: The existence of an opponent before the creation of the creatures, and his coming to the creatures
9.20: after, the creation of the creatures, and also to the creator, are presented comprehensibly through reasons which are suitable and presentable, and through the provision of a remedy, a creation which is for a purpose.
9.21: This one statement (vâkak) possesses five arguments (sâmân).
9.22: One is the being presented comprehensibly.
9.23: One is the being presented through reasons.
9.24: One is the reasons which are presentable and suitable that the creation existed.
9.25: One is the remedy appointed for the creation.
9.26: And one is the creation of the creatures of the creator for a purpose.
9.27: The existence of these five arguments is manifest through the creations and achievements themselves.
9.28: The presenting comprehensibly is wisely arranging the testimony of the effect of the creatures,
9.29: through the reasons presented, which are a declaration owing to the same sagacity.
9.30: The reason obtainable, that the creation existed,
9.31: with the arrangement of the creation so methodically, ought to arise from the suitable state of the creation;
9.32: and the suitable design of the creation itself possesses the testimony, through its appearance.
9.33: The remedy appointed is a comprehensible and presentable demonstrator,
9.34: because it becomes a desire of knowledge and an appearance of the desire.
9.35: The being created for a purpose is manifest through the desire of activity of the creation, both severally and naturally.
9.36: The evidences of the existence of an opponent before the creation of the creatures are many.
9.37: And one of them is the suitable state of the creation of the creatures,
9.38: because the limit of suitability is not well fitted for anything except necessity.
9.39: That which is inferred from suitability is necessity, from necessity haste, and from haste the existence of an opponent who is before the suitable work which is the creation.
9.40: The evidence of the coming of the destroyer to the creatures, after the creation of the creatures, is the formation of the means of the creator, for encountering an opponent, before the arrival of the opponent,
9.41: which are omnisciently a provision before creation by the creator.
9.42: And there is a demonstrator of these same means of the creatures that is prepared, which is the struggling opposed to the opponent through the arrangement of their nature.
9.43: One duty of the nature of the creatures is the subduing of so much vexation.
9.44: Their preparation, too, is like a contest that is forming an enemy opposing the opponent,
9.45: and their natural desire for duty is removing all haste.

10.1: Another subject is about the deliberating of the deliberators on unity, from which even the preparation of the duality is manifested.
10.2: It should be known, that whoever wishes to understand a creator, except when he gives trouble to his own life,
10.4: First, he fully understands his own body and soul,
10.5: that is, who produced them, out of what, and for what purpose?
10.6: Also, who is his accuser and adversary;
10.7: and who is his friend and helper?
10.8: Likewise, who instigates him to commit crime,
10.10: and how is it possible to escape him?
10.11: Then he is not able to understand him as the creator through his nature and his coming to himself.
10.12: For when he bore the name of creator, then, with it, he brought these three creations:—
10.14: Because the name of creator is known from the occurrence of creation.
10.15: This implies that the creator of the creation created the creations for duty,
10.16: but does not release them from duty.
10.17: And the duty of the creatures is to understand and perform the will of the creator,
10.18: and to abstain from what is disliked by him.
10.19: To act by the will of the creator, and to abstain from what is disliked by him, is to preserve the soul.
10.20: The will of the creator is not understood, except from the religion of the creator.
10.21: And the religion is appointed by the creator free from doubt.
10.22: Now it is expedient to know that the sacred being appointed the religion for the understanding of his will,
10.23: and from the understanding of his will for the preservation of the soul are manifested the compassion and mercifulness of the sacred being.
10.24: From the preservativeness of the religion for the soul are manifested the grandeur and valuableness of the religion;
10.25: from the necessity of preserving the soul are manifested the defilement and delusion of the soul;
10.26: and from the defilement and delusion of the soul is manifested a defiler and deluder of the thoughts, words, and deeds of mankind.
10.27: On the whole a corrupter of souls is manifest.
10.28: And now it is expedient for us to well recognise and know, as to that defiler who is a corrupter of souls, of what nature he is.
10.29: Because, if the creation and achievement of the sacred being are said to be of a like nature, then how did the sacred being appoint the religion for the preservation of the soul?
10.30: That is not expedient for him—if a defiler and deluder of souls—to produce as his own creation and will.
10.31: For if he be himself the creator, and be himself the defiler and corrupter of souls, and nothing occurs except by his will,
10.32: then, when it is necessary for us to write of preservation from the sacred being, whom shall we make as a refuge?
10.33: Now it is necessary for every intelligent person to understand and to know thus much,
10.34: that is, from whom it is necessary for us to flee and to abstain,
10.35: and with whom is the hope, and with whom the maintenance, of our protection.
10.36: The method for this acquisition is nothing else but to understand the sacred being in his nature,
10.37: because, as I wrote above, it is not only to know his existence, but it is necessary to understand his nature and his will.
10.38: And I have observed, in the world, the sectarian belief of all maintainers of sects who hold [the two fundamental doctrines].
10.39: One is that which asserts that all the good and evil, which are in the world, are owing to the sacred being.
10.40: And one is that which asserts that all the good of the world, besides the hope of preserving the soul, is owing to the sacred being;
10.41: and the cause of all evil of the body, besides the risk of the soul, is owing to Aharman;
10.42: and all things have started from appointment by these two origins into various formations and various subdivisions.
10.43: Now I have been an enquirer everywhere, for understanding the sacred being, as written above, fervent-minded in the investigation of his religion and will;
10.44: as likewise I have wandered, for the sake of investigation, to the region without and the land of the Hindûs, and to many different races.
10.45: Because, as to religion, I did not admire that which was in supremacy,
10.46: but I sought that which was more steadfast and more acceptable in wisdom and testimony.
10.47: I went also into association with many different races,
10.49: when, owing to the compassion of the sacred beings, and the strength, glory, and power of the good religion, I escaped from much gloomy depth and ill-solvable doubt.
10.50: By the united power of knowledge of the religion
10.51: and the well-reflecting writing of the wise,
10.52: the marvellous allegorical writings of the learned Âtûr-pâdîyâvand,
10.53: and by that writing which the glorified Rôshan, son of Âtûr-frôbag, prepared—
10.54: for which he appointed the name of the Rôshan manuscript (nipîk)—
10.55: and likewise that for which the supremely learned and righteous Âtûr-frôbag, son of Farukh-zâd,
10.56: who was the leader of those of the good religion,
10.57: appointed the name of the Dînkard manuscript—owing to its explaining the religion —
10.58: I am saved from the many doubts, delusions, deceits, and follies of sects,
10.59: and, especially, from those of the deceivers, the very great and very mighty, very evil-teaching and empty-skulled Manicheans,
10.60:
whose devotion is witchcraft, whose religion is deceitfulness, and whose teaching is folly and intricate secret proceedings.
61. I have been deliberately confirmed by the power of wisdom and the strength of knowledge of the religion,
10.62: not through obstinate faith, but by the pure revelation opposed to the demon, which is the decision of Aûharmazd
10.63:
that was taught by the creator Aûharmazd to the righteous Zaratûst.
64. Zaratûst came alone, on a true mission, to the lofty portal of Kaî Gustâsp,
10.65:
and the religion was taught by him, with a powerful tongue, to Kaî Gustâsp and the learned, through the speech of wisdom, through manual gestures, through definite words, through explanation of many doubts, and through presentation of the visible testimony of the archangels, together with many miracles. 66. And a greatness in power which is not the destiny of worldly existences was theirs who saw him of the vehement guardian spirit. 67. And Kaî Spend-dâd and Zargar and other royal sons (zâdak), instigating the many conflicts and shedding the blood of those of the realm, accepted the religion as a yoke, (68) while they even wandered to Arûm and the Hindûs, outside the realm, in propagating the religion.
69. Owing to progress onwards it came in succession to the descendants of the divinities, the rulers who were those of the Kayân race who were exalted ones. 70. And still onwards even until the achievement with melted metal pouring upon the chest of the glorified Âtûr-pâd, son of Mâraspend, in the reign of that divinity (bagh) Shâhpûr, the king of kings who was the son of Aûharmazd, in a controversy with apostates of different species of many kinds. 71. He was preserved from those most mighty apostates, who are called even by the name of their desires.
72. And the Arûmans, who have been, at various periods, termed untruthful, have asked many ill-solvable questions of this religion; (73) but there has been no doubtfulness of any question that is explained by this religion, (74) and the learned of the country of Irân have always been sustainers of victory among them. 75. Not like other sects whose religion is secretly progressive and deceiving, delusively for the deceived, and undutifully among the customs and assemblages of the less-informed, unintelligent, and demon-natured whose information was nothing whatever of knowledge and understanding of wisdom. 76. Then, so far as the assemblages that are very secretly deceived and deluded by them, nobody is presented for detection (âskârâkîh); (77) but afterwards, owing to the capture of the many of little knowledge and unintelligent opinions who are deluded by them, it is discovered they are provided with much mutually afflicting speech, falsehood, and disconnection, which are their religion.
78. So that I here notice some of their much inconsistency and disconnection, for informing the judgment of new learners, (79) for the reason that when the writings of the learned ancients have specially minutely and reverently discoursed of what is most astute in evil, to impel one to good knowledge, (80) you should observe with kind regards what is ordered.

11.1: Henceforth I write of the inconsistency of their twaddle, and of just observations
11.2: you should estimate with wise regard.
11.3: First, as to the full consideration of that one original evolution
11.4: which they state thus: 'The sacred being is one, doing good works, wise, powerful, compassionate, and merciful,
11.5: so that good works and crime, truth and falsehood, life and death, good and evil are owing to him.'
11.6: Now do ye ask of them
11.7: thus: 'Is the sacred being always compassionate and showing mercy, doing good works and judicious, and does he know all that is, was, and will be; and is he advancing the desire of one's wishes in everything, even in this where judiciousness is interference, or when such is not so?
11.8: Because, if he be compassionate, doing good works, and showing mercy, why then are Aharman and the demons and all these evil faiths of hell admitted by him to his own creatures, through his own compassion, doing of good works, and showing of mercy?
11.9: If not known by him, where are that knowledge and omniscience of his?
11.10: If he did not wish to keep misery and evil away from the creatures, and to produce only happiness for every one, where are that judiciousness and interference of his?
11.11: If it were not possible that it should not be produced by him, for what is that omnipotence of his
11.12: which we every one, as it were, observe and well consider?'
11.13: Whenever they say that every good and evil has arisen from the sacred being—except when they separate from him these four attributes (hûnar), requisite for divinity, which are omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and mercifulness—
11.14: there is then no possibility of it.
11.15: When, indeed, they separate from him only one of these four attributes, even then he is not complete in divinity.
11.16: For if a sacred being be he who is omniscient, omnipotent, good, and merciful, then he who is not omniscient, or not omnipotent, or not good, or not merciful is not a sacred being.
11.17: Again, observe this, that when he is a ruler, advancing desires in every person and thing, why are that country and empire of his own not so kept, without help, from every enemy and adversity apart from his own work, so that there would not be anything whatever of distress, oppression, injustice, and complaint for any one in his empire?
11.18: Since the rule and empire of a man, who is ruler and emperor, are then commendable when it is possible for him so to protect and keep his own country and empire, through his own wisdom, that they may not assist his enemy to detract from his work, and to produce sin and harm.
11.19: Or, when his enemy covets some of his work, he is enabled to keep him away from his own thoughtful friends, and to make every one free from distress.
11.20: Again, observe this, that when he is triumphant, victorious, and prevailing,
11.21: over whom are that triumph, victory, and prevailing of his?
11.22: Since triumph and victory are over enemies, a competitor exists.
11.23: It is not expedient to become himself a competitor and enemy to his own;
11.24: while when there is no enemy and competitor of his, over whom does he become triumphant and victorious?
11.25: That sort of triumph and victory is not spoken about,
11.26: because even cattle and sheep, when they have no opponent and injurer, are victorious and triumphant over themselves.
11.27: Again, observe this, is a wise being contented with his own divinity and grandeur, or not?
11.28: If the wise being be contented, then he has become contented to produce an enemy and criminal, and to admit all that is devastating into a country, through his own knowledge and will, for the benefit of the country and creatures.
11.29: But why is it expedient to seek a disposition of crime and evil, to become himself an enemy and curser as regards them, and to provide a hellish existence, becoming the misery of mankind?
11.30: Again, observe this, as to whatever he says, does he speak truly and credibly, or not?
11.31: If he speaks that truly and credibly which he states thus: 'I am a friend of good works and an enemy of crime,'
11.32: and always produces more crime and criminals than good works and doers of good works,
11.33: where is that truthful speaking of his?
11.34: Again, observe this, is his desire goodness, or vileness?
11.35: If his desire be vileness, whence is that divinity of his?
11.36: If his desire be goodness, then why are the vile and vileness more than the good and goodness?
11.37: Again, observe this, is he merciful, or not?
11.38: If he be not merciful, whence is that divinity of his?
11.39: If he be merciful, then why does he speak thus: 'The hearts, ears, and eyes of mankind are bent about by me, so that it is not possible for them to think, speak, or do anything but that which is wanted by me;
11.40: be it what has made them great and noble, through being without want;
11.41: or be it what has admitted them to eternal hell, slain and exterminated by death of many kinds.
11.42: So that while those whom I force back become good and more active in good works,
11.43: yet still those who are forced back do only a little,
11.44: and are much more criminal and more sinful than those who are forward.'
11.45: Again, observe this, that if, whatever he does, he does wisely and for a purpose,
11.46: then, when no opponent and adversary of his existed, why did the first achievement which was prepared by him become servants to demoniacal disobedience, who are perverted thereby, among mankind, to wickedness and a hellish existence?
11.47: If it were not known by him that they would become perverted, it was expedient (sazîd) for him to order the making of a trial of them,
11.48: because now many thousands and myriads who are prepared by him, so that they may serve him and exhilarate (mastend) his rule, have become in every mode disobedient and unhappily advised.
11.49: for with that scanty knowledge that mankind possess, which is not so prepared and organized as is the wish of mankind,
11.50: if even anything arises, that they construct and prepare, which does not so come on and become as is their wish, they do not stop again, a second time, for the preparation of that thing, but they refrain from it.
11.51: As to him, that omnipotent and omniscient ruler, of the abundant and innumerable things he has hitherto made and prepared not even one comes on and becomes such as is his wish, yet still he never refrains from the preparation and production of many new things.
11.52: Just as when he was the creator of that one of his first angels whom, on account of affection, he prepared out of fire, and for several thousand years,
11.53: as they say, they always performed his worship;
11.54: at last that one was undone by one command that was given by him (the creator) thus: 'Offer homage to this first of mankind, who is prepared by me out of clay.'
11.55: And deliverance, as to what is not expedient to offer, was expressly mentioned by him.
11.56: Then that one acted scornfully and contemptibly as to his clay and curse and wrath;
11.57: and, being perverted to devilry and fiendishness, he was forced out of heaven,
11.58: and was given a life of millenniums and an eternal dominion,
11.59: so that he said, 'I will go and make my servants and worshippers astray and deluded.'
11.60: And he was made an injurer and adversary at his own will.
11.61: At last also that man, to whom he, the supreme angel, was ordered to offer homage with many worshippers, for the sake of affection and respect,
11.62: is appointed to the garden of paradise (vahist),
11.63: so that he may cultivate it and eat all the fruit,
11.64: except of that one tree of which it is ordered thus: Ye shall not eat of it.'
11.65: And with them (mankind) the deceiver, who is the deluder prepared by him (the creator),
11.67: There are some who say he is a serpent, and there are some who say he is Aharman.
11.68: And an inclination for eating and greediness is given by that same one himself to mankind.
11.69: Then, being deceived by that deluder saying: 'Eat of that tree'—
11.70: there are some who say he spoke to Adam—
11.71: they ate through that inclination for eating.
11.72: After eating they became so imbued with knowledge that good and evil were understood and known by them.
11.73: Deprived of that so-great respect and affection, through that one injunction which was forgotten by them—
11.74: and that forgetfulness being likewise owing to that cause—
11.75: they are forced out of the garden of paradise —he with his wife—by grievous wrath and disrespect,
11.76: and are delivered into the hand of that enemy who is a deceiver and deluder;
11.77: so that he has propagated his own will among them, and has fashioned it upon them.
11.78: Now which was unjust, the unreasonable command, the after-wisdom, or the scanty knowledge that was more faulty and more mischievous than these?
11.79: Also this, that is, why was that garden not made by him fortified and strong, so that that deluder could not have gone into it?
11.80: Even now he (the deceiver) has made and makes multitudes of his (the creator's) servants and worshippers deluded;
11.81: and, for the same reason, multitudes of apostles and prophets (vakhshvarân) are appointed by him (the creator) for the worldly existence at various times,
11.82: so that, as he says: 'They may save my servants from the hand of that deluder,
11.83: and bring them into the true path and way.'
11.84: And even those worshippers of his, in every way through their own will, have slain and subdued (khvâft), by a wretched death, his own apostles, whose diligence had brought mankind into the proper path and doctrine.
11.85: That original deluder and misleader is allowed an eternal life.
11.86: And, even till now, his will is more triumphant and absolute than that of the sacred being, through deluding and misleading,
11.87: because those deluded and astray are much more numerous than those in the true path and undeluded.
11.88: Again, observe this, does he do whatever he does for a purpose, or not?
11.89: If he does it without a purpose, he is working foolishly;
11.90: and it is not proper to praise him who is working foolishly as a sagacious divinity.
11.91: If he does it for a purpose,
11.92: then, when no opponent and adversary of his existed, why is the production of all these creatures which are even like demons, disobedient men with the opposing will of that contentious deluder, and innumerable unprofitable creatures?
11.93: Again, observe this, that, if he knows all that is, was, and will be, it was not expedient for him to produce, through his own knowledge and will, anything of that of which he may be sorry, and which remains opposing his will and command,
11.94: and becomes an adversary of his apostles and the doers of his will.
11.95: If they say that this adversary was produced good and virtuous from the beginning, and afterwards became an evil and a misleading of the creatures,
11.96: that implies, you should say, that, when he is all-powerful, the purpose and will of the adversary, in changing into an evil and a misleading of the creatures, are more successful and more powerful than those of the sacred being;
11.97: because the evil in any period is stronger than the good.
11.98: Again, observe this, that when a criminal arises wholly through his will,
11.99: and the minds of criminals are defiled by him himself,
11.100: and the seed of crime is sown by him himself,
11.101:
when it has grown who has maintained its origin? 102.
And by what power of adjudication is one executed and one rewarded?
11.103: Again, observe this, was this world made and created by him (the creator) for a purpose, for his own pleasure and for the sake of the comfort and happiness of mankind, or without a purpose, for his own discomfort and the hurry, trouble, pain, and death of mankind?
11.104: For if made by him without a purpose, he was acting foolishly;
11.105: a thing without a purpose being not acceptable by the wise.
11.106: If made by him for a purpose, and created by him for his own pleasure and the comfort and happiness of mankind,
11.107: why was it not made by him prosperous and full of happiness?
11.108: If his pleasure and happiness arise from the preparation of mankind and the creatures, what is the advantage from their slaughter and devastation?
11.109: If thoughts of crime are not given by him himself to mankind, who is he who gives thoughts of crime different from his command and will?
11.110: If they are given by him himself, and he now considers them a fault, what is that justice and arbitration of his owing to?
11.111: For when mankind, with little knowledge and little wisdom, even then, so far as they are able, do not let the lion and wolf and other noxious creatures in among their own young ones and pregnant females,
11.112: so long as they can destroy them,
11.113: why has the merciful sacred being now let Aharman and the demons in upon his own creatures,
11.114: so that they have made them vile, defiled, wicked, and hellish?
11.115: If done for the sake of experiment, just as that which they assert, that evil was created by him for the sake of an experiment as regards the creatures,
11.116: why was it not understood by him before those men and creatures existed?
11.117: Because he whose custom is experiment is not to be called omniscient.
11.118: The conclusion is this, that the sacred being, if there existed no opponent and adversary of his, was able to create all those creatures and creations of his free from misfortune; why did he not so create them?
11.119: Or was it not possible for him to wish it?
11.120: If it were not possible for him to wish it, he is not completely capable.
11.121: If it were possible for him not to wish it, he is not merciful.
11.122: If it were known by him that he might say: 'Something or some one will arise, from these creatures and creations which I create, that will not be according to my will,'
11.124: then to attach now all this wrath and cursing and casting away for punishment in hell, discontentedly to his own performance, is unreasonable.
11.125: Again, observe this, that if all the crime-meditating and crime-committing sin which mankind think and speak and do, as well as pain, sickness, poverty, and the punishment and misery of hell, cannot arise, except by the will and command of the sacred being—
11.126: the will and power of the sacred being being eternal,
11.127: because his self-existence is also eternal—
11.128: the hopelessness of eternally saving any one whatever from misery and punishment is now certain.
11.129: For it is repeatedly declared that there is no learned teacher whatever who keeps one away from these mischievous evil desires,
11.130: if the worshipper be even of the same kind as those worshippers and high-priests who have issued to mankind this admonition: 'Commit no crime and sin.'
11.131: Because they wish to set aside the will and command of the sacred being.
11.132: Observe this, too, that, as both are his will, alike crime and alike good works, it is not manifest whether he approves the good works of doers of good works more, or the crimes of criminals.
11.133: Likewise observe this, those physicians who, on account of the hope of the soul, prepare the medicine of the sick,
11.134: and remove and dismiss their pain and disease, (115) so that merit is possessed by them (the physicians) owing to that practice;
11.136: yet they are prepared for the punishment of hell.
11.137: And those who, on account of affection for the soul, give something to poor, begging, suffering people,
11.138: and thereby scatter and dismiss their want and poverty,
11.139: so that merit is possessed by them (the charitable) owing to that practice;
11.140: yet it becomes grievous sin for them, through anxiety.
11.141: If they say that those physicians and the remedies which they offer, and also those who give something to the poor and suffering, all exist by the will of the sacred being,
11.142: it is easier, more reasonable, and more adapted to divinity, when the sacred being is without an adversary and without an opponent, for him not to create that disease and poverty
11.143: than that, as to those that he himself is to make sick and poor, he should have commanded mankind thus: 'Ye shall make them healthy and free from want.'
11.144: If they say that his desire is this, that he may occasion the happiness of those physicians and givers by the recompense for it,
11.145: and make them proceed to the eternal happiness of heaven (vahist);
11.146: you should observe, as to that, since he acts injudiciously and incapably when, on account of the existence of a complete desire for happiness and prosperity among others, he is an attainer of misery for multitudes of the innocent who are distressed, poor, necessitous, and sick,
11.147: this may also be said, that if it be not possible for him to occasion happiness and prosperity as regards one, except by the distress, pain, and vexation of some other,
11.148: that shows that his absolute power and freedom from opposition are not adapted for effectual operation.
11.149: If they say that he makes those sick and poor proceed to the eternal happiness of heaven in the spiritual existence, as a recompense for it,
11.150: that implies, if it be not possible, or not completely possible, for him to give the recompense in the spiritual existence, except through the misery of the worldly one,
11.151: also this, that—his production of distress in the worldly existence arising unquestionably and unreasonably, through its previous occurrence,
11.152: and the recompense of the spiritual existence arising doubtfully and incredibly after the production of the distress—
11.153: just as the previous distress is unreasonable, the after recompense occurs alike unreasonably and foolishly.
11.154: This also may be said, that no after nobility is obtained for previous distress without a cause.
11.155: Again, observe this, that the existence of one of these three doctrines is inevitable:—
11.156: Every single thing that is, or was, or will be in this world is all by his will, or it is not,
11.157: or there are some that are by his will and there are some that are not.
11.158: Because nothing whatever is found which is not good, or evil, or a mixture of both.
11.159: If they say that all things are by his will, the good and evil are both his desire.
11.160: If good and evil are both his desire, he is not of perfect will;
11.161: it is not perfect even as to a single thing.
11.162: And he who is of imperfect will must be himself imperfect,
11.164: If nothing be by his will,
11.165: on account of nothing being by the will there is no will.
11.166: He in whom there is no will is working constitutionally,
11.167: and he who is working constitutionally is constituted and made.
11.168: If there be some things which are by his will, and there be some which are not by his will,
11.169: and nothing is found in the world which is not good and not evil,
11.170: from that it is known that, if the sacred being be of good will, he is not desirous of that evil of it,
11.171: and that which is evil is not by his will.
11.172: If his will be evil he is inevitably not desirous of that good of it,
11.173: and that which is good is not by his will.
11.174: If that which is good be by the will of the sacred being, it is known that that which is evil arose from another will.
11.175: If that which is evil be by his will, that which is good arose inevitably from another will.
11.176: And the inevitability of a rival of the will of the sacred being is manifest.
11.177: If one says the evil springs from mankind,
11.178: that implies the inevitability—since mankind is not perpetually a self-existence—that evil either arose before mankind, or after,
11.180: If they say it arose before mankind,
11.181: that implies—since, apart from the sacred being, there was no other creator and producer
11.182: that either the sacred being produced that evil, or it produced its own existence itself, or it was itself eternal.
11.183: If they say it arose after mankind,
11.184: as to that, when human nature is likewise a production of the sacred being,
11.185: and the sacred being did not produce evil in the nature of mankind,
11.186: how has it sprung into action from them?
11.187: If the evil was set in action by them, apart from the will of the sacred being,
11.188: and a knowledge, as to their setting about it, existed in the sacred being,
11.189: that implies that the sacred being is imperfect in his own will,
11.190: and mankind are victorious and triumphant in setting aside the will and command of the sacred being, and doing the evil competing with the will of the sacred being.
11.191: Also the power of the sacred being in his own will and his own servants is manifestly unprevailing.
11.192: If they say that he makes them proceed afterwards to the awful punishment of hell,
11.193: as to that, if the sacred being be a powerful doer, and not to allow the committal of crime, but to convey it away from their minds, be more advantageous and more adapted to the compassion of a sacred being than if he allowed the committal,
11.194: yet he has become helplessly contented with it,
11.195: and, afterwards, contentedly punishes his own creatures,
11.196: then, as to the one matter I am well considering, either incapability, or scanty knowledge, or scanty goodness is thereby manifested.
11.197: If they say that the sacred being produced and created evil for the reason that so mankind may fully understand the value of goodness,
11.198: as to that you should observe that, if evil be requisite and advantageous for understanding goodness, that evil exists by his good will.
11.199: And if evil exists by his good will, and is requisite and advantageous for him of whom they say that evil is not his wish, it is inconsistent.
11.200: As to that also which they say, that death, pain, and poverty are produced by him for the reason that so mankind may much better understand the value of life, health, and opulence,
11.201: and become more grateful unto the sacred being,
11.202: as to that you should observe that it is as it were acting unreasonably, in the mode of him who gives poison to mankind for the sake of increasing the value and price of an antidote,
11.203: so that he may sell the antidote dearer and more costly.
11.204: To what is this intermeddling action owing, that, for the sake of an understanding of the value of the goodness of other things, he allows pain, death, and misery in some one else?
11.205: Again, as to that which a multitude of them say, that the sacred being is a ruler over every creature and creation,
11.206: because his creations are all his own.
11.207: And he acts about them as is desirable for him, because it is desirable for him, and he is not a causer of distress.
11.208: Since distress is that which they inflict upon anything that is not their own,
11.209: then the who, all things being his own, acts about them as is desirable for him, is not a causer of distress.
11.210: As to that you should know that, if, on account of sovereignty, he who occasions distress is not to be called a causer of distress,
11.211: that is as though even he who is a sovereign and tells a lie is speaking truthfully,
11.212: and he who, on account of sovereignty, commits crime, sin, theft, and plunder is not to be called a sinner.
11.213: Such as that which the glorified Rôshan, son of Âtûr-frôbag, related as a parable (ângunî-aîtak),
11.214: that they saw a man who was defiling an ass,
11.215: when they enquired of him thus: 'Why dost thou commit this execrable action?'
11.216: And he spoke thus, in excuse: 'The ass is my own.'
11.217: Again, you should ask this of them,
11.218: that is: 'Is the sacred being a friend, or an enemy, to these creatures and creations which are made by him?'
11.219: If he be a friend of the creatures, that implies that it is not proper for him to desire and to produce the evil and misery of the creatures;
11.220: yet, as regards the devastation and misery of his own achievements, he has never even become tired of them.
11.221: If he be an enemy of the creatures, that implies that it is not proper for him to create and produce, through his own competent knowledge, that thing which is his enemy and disablement, and struggles against his will.
11.223: that is: 'Is the sacred being always a well-understanding, good sovereign, occasioning prosperity,
11.224: or an evil-understanding, bad sovereign, occasioning distress?
11.225: Or is there a time when he is a well-understanding, good sovereign, occasioning prosperity,
11.226: and is there a time when he is an evil-understanding, bad sovereign, occasioning distress?'
11.227: If he be always a well-understanding, good sovereign, occasioning prosperity,
11.228: that implies that there are not, in his country and sovereignty, any oppression, distress, and complaint;
11.229: and his affection for the creatures and the affection of the creatures for him are pure.
11.230: Owing to the same reason he is merciful as regards his own creatures,
11.231: and his creatures are recounting his praise, utterers of thanksgivings and pure friends towards him.
11.232: His title of divinity, moreover, is worthily his own.
11.233: If he be an evil-understanding, bad sovereign, occasioning distress,
11.234: that implies that he is himself a pure enemy to the creatures, and his creatures are also of a like nature towards him.
11.235: Owing to the same reason he is an injurer, destroyer, and deluder of the creatures,
11.236: and his creatures are complainers of him, strugglers concerning him, and pure enemies.
11.237: His title of divinity, moreover, is the equivalent of an unworthy name;
11.238: and, even on account of his eternity, the creatures are hopeless of becoming free from the risk of distress and misery for an unlimited time.
11.239: If there be a time when he is a good sovereign, well-understanding, and occasioning prosperity, and there be a time when he is turned away from this;
11.240: that implies that his affection for the creatures is mingled.
11.241: From a mingled affection arises mingled action,
11.242: and from mingled action a mingled individuality is also manifested.
11.243: And his creatures also are mingled friends to him.
11.244: Of one's associates there is none who, if a friend, is not one's enemy, no praiser who is not complaining of one, no glorifier even who is not scorning one; a character of this description is manifest among all creatures.
11.245: Again, observe this, that since all things which are in the world are not outside of these two terms, good and evil,
11.246: that implies, if good and evil are both said to arise from the sacred being and through the will of the sacred being,
11.247: that the troublesome Aharman is unreasonably defamed; that, being innocent and without an original evolution, he never was, nor will be, evil and headstrong.
11.248: That which is mentioned in scripture (nipîk), that Aharman became headstrong, and was put out of heaven by them, is unreasonable,
11.249: because even that headstrongness and disobedience were likewise through the will of the sacred being.
11.250: If even it be said that the good arises from the sacred being and through the will of the sacred being, and the evil from mankind, still Aharman is without an original evolution and innocent, and curses and scorn for him are unreasonable.
11.251: If all this misery and evil be sent down, not from a different nature, but from the individuality and individual nature of the sacred being himself,
11.252: that implies that the sacred being is an enemy and adversary to his own tendencies (rûn).
11.253: Observe this, too, that to speak of the existence of criminality apart from a nature of crime is very deluding;
11.254: and as it is deluding to imagine a nature of crime that is good, is it more deluding to imagine Aharman—who is the origin and original evolution of every crime—apart from the creation and achievement of the sacred being?
11.255: The conclusion is this, that if at first there be anything which is not within the will of the sacred being, provided everything be through the will of the sacred being, no one whatever is a sinner;
11.256: and the apostle and religion were appointed without a purpose.
11.257: If it be expedient to ruin any one for sinfulness, it is more expedient to ruin him who is the original doer, maintainer, and creator of every evil and crime.
11.258: And if it be said that evil and crime arise from Aharman or mankind, that implies, as they are likewise created and produced by the sacred being, that he is the source of them; in like manner, he who is the cause of the origin of evil
11.260: This, too, you should observe, that sects (kêshân) of every kind assert this maxim, handed down by their own high-priests, when it is mentioned and prescribed by them to their own congregation (ram), that is: 'Perform good works and abstain from crime.'
11.261: On account of delusion they do not consider this, that is, from where and what origin ought the crime to arise, about which it is thus commanded: 'Ye shall not commit it, and I will cast him who commits it into eternal hell.'
11.262: So that, if that same be owing to the sacred being, it would be easier for him not to produce it, than, after its production, to have brought it to notice and commanded us to abstain from it.
11.263: So far, indeed, I do not understand any advantage and motive in the production and creation of evil.
11.264: Again, in their scriptures, he speaks inconsistently about good works and crime
11.265: thus: 'Good works and crime are both owing to me.
11.266: Neither demons, nor wizards, are unrestricted in causing the ruin of any one.
11.267: No one has accepted the religion and done good works, and no one has walked in infidelity and committed crime, except through my will.'
11.268: In the same scripture he adduces many things which one has to connect, and inflicts curses on the creatures,
11.269: thus: 'Why do mankind desire and commit that crime which I design for them?'
11.270: It occurs concerning the will and work of his own hand, and yet he frightens them with punishment in body and soul.
11.271: In another place he speaks thus: 'I myself am the deluder of mankind, for if it should be my will they would then be shown the true path by me, but it is my will that they go to hell.'
11.272: And in another place he speaks thus: 'Man himself is the causer of crime.'
11.273: In these three modes the sacred being gives evidence of different kinds about his own creatures.
11.274: One is this, that he himself is Aharman;
11.275: one is this, that he is himself the deluder of the creatures;
11.276: and, in the other, he makes his own creatures confederates involved with Aharman in deluding; so that he implies: 'There are instances when I occasion it, and there are instances when Aharman does.'
11.277: Through that which he states, that mankind themselves occasion crime, they are made by him confederates with Aharman; he himself being at a distance from the crime.
11.278:
For if mankind commit crime owing to their own nature and their own delusion, that implies that the sacred being, with
Aharman, is far from the criminality,
11.279: because it is as it were not owing to the sacred being, nor yet owing to Aharman.
11.280: Again, you should ask of those whom they call Mûtazalîk
11.281: thus: 'Is it the will of the sacred being for all mankind to abstain from crime through their own free will, to escape from hell, and to make them proceed to heaven, or not?'
11.282: If one says that it is not,
11.283: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to the little goodness of the sacred being and the evil of his will;
11.284: and, for the same reason, it is not fitting to glorify him as the divine existence.
11.285: If one says that it is his will,
11.286: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to the good will of the sacred being;
11.287: and, for the same reason, it is fitting to glorify him as the divine existence.
11.288: Ask this, too, that is: 'If it be his will, is he capable of performing it, or not?'
11.289: If one says that he is not,
11.290: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to the incapability of the sacred being as regards that will of his;
11.291: and, for the same reason, it is not fitting to glorify him as the divine existence which is almighty.
11.292: If one says that he is capable of performing his will,
11.293: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to his capability for that will of his;
11.294: and, for the same reason, it is fitting to glorify him as the divine existence which is almighty.
11.295: Again, ask this, that is: 'When he is capable of performing his will, does he perform it, or not?'
11.296: If one says that he performs it,
11.297: that implies that the abstaining from sin, escaping from hell, and bringing to heaven would be manifested unto all mankind;
11.298: but this is that which is not manifest by his existence, and is falsifying even his own revelation (dînŏ).
11.299: If one says that he is capable of performing his will, but does not perform it,
11.300: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to the unmercifulness of the sacred being, his enmity to mankind, and the inconstancy of his will.
11.301: For if he performs it, it is no harm to him himself and is an advantage to mankind; his own will is also continuous thereby.
11.302: But if he does not perform it, it is no advantage to him himself and, is harm to mankind; his own will is also discontinuous thereby.
11.303: Again, ask this, that is: 'Does he not perform it through will, or without will?'
11.304: If one says that he does not perform it through will,
11.305: that implies that an opinion is formed by him that the sacred being is good-willed, but has no will to do good;
11.306: and this is even to consider him faulty through inconsistency.
11.307: If one says that he is without will, and therefore does not perform it,
11.308: that implies that an opinion is formed by him as to the weakness of the sacred being in his own self, or the existence of an injurer of his will.
11.309: The conclusion is this, that, with a manager of this worldly existence who may be without an opponent, without competition, and perfect in sagacity, goodness, and capability, there should not be all these unworthy actions, trouble and misery, pain and vexation, especially of mankind and the other creatures.
11.310: Because, when a manager, without an opponent, is perfect in sagacity, he knows means for evil not to occur and also remedies for carrying off evil.
11.311: When he is perfect in goodness and merciful, he has no wish for the occurrence of evil at first, but a wish for its extinction.
11.312: When he is perfect in capability, he is capable of not really becoming equally the origin of evil.
11.313: Now, as in the worldly existence, whose manager is the sacred being, the existence of evil is unquestionably visible, then thus much is not separable from this, either where the manager is provided with an opponent, or is without an opponent:—314. If he does not know means for evil not to occur, and remedies for carrying off evil, the imperfect sagacity of the sacred being is thereby manifested.
11.315: Or the evil exists with his good will, and the imperfect goodness of his will is manifested.
11.316: Or he is not capable of not allowing the occurrence of evil, and of carrying it off, and the imperfect capability of the sacred being is manifested.
11.317: And when he is imperfect even in one—in sagacity, or goodness, or capability—it is not fitting to glorify and worship him as the divine existence who is almighty, all-good, and all-wise.
11.318: This, too, you should know, that since any existing thing, which is acting, is provided with a will, but its nature has not become unrestricted,
11.319: that shows that, if the original existence of the creator be divinity, and his nature be light and beauty, fragrance and purity, goodness and sagacity, then such things as darkness and ugliness, stench and pollution, vileness and ignorance—the demoniacal nature itself—ought to be far from him.
11.320: If his original existence be anything demoniacal, and his nature be darkness or stench, ugliness or pollution, vileness or ignorance, then the nature of divinity remains strange to him.
11.321: If there be any one by whom indecision about all this is insinuated into his own self, that implies that, owing to his indecision about it, there is no discrimination in him as to goodness, amid his own evil.
11.322: Now, moreover, the hope of the hopeful is absorbed,
11.323: for even he who goes to heaven through doing good works is, even there, in evil and misery,
11.324: because there is no distinct discrimination of good from evil, even there,
11.325: if there be the goodness which is devoid of evil, and there be also the evil which is devoid of goodness, represented as really of the same origin.
11.326: This is known, that the difference of good and evil is owing to difference of nature.
11.327: When the two origins of their difference and distinction from the other of different nature are manifest, that hope of the hopeful is just,
11.329: This, too, you should know, that every statement which is not unconfused by its own limits is unenquiring (apad-khvâh).
11.330: Likewise this, that the limit of divinity is specially sagacity.
11.331: And also this, that the limit of sagacity is only advantageous action.
11.332: Advantageous action is not doing injury;
11.333: and the modes of doing injury are three.
11.334: One is that which, being no advantage to oneself, is the injury of another also.
11.335: [One is that which, being no advantage to another ], is the injury of oneself also.
11.336: And one is that which is the injury of oneself and the injury of another also.
11.337: And from the creation of Aharman and the demons there is no advantage to a wisely-acting sacred being himself, and there is injury of others also;
11.338: the non-advancement of even his own will, owing to his own work, is always manifested thereby.
11.339: This, too, you should know, that if the will of the sacred being be goodness,
11.341: And he should be capable of a suitable will,
11.342: so that, from the beginning even to the end, all the goodness and virtue of the will of the sacred being would have proceeded in the world.
11.343: Now it is manifest that vileness and vice always proceed much more.
11.344: Therefore the cause is one of these, either they always proceed through the will of the sacred being, or without his will.
11.345: If they always proceed through some will of the sacred being, it is evident that his will is also for vileness as well as for goodness,
11.346: or he is inefficient and changeable in will.
11.347: Since a will does not change, unless owing to a cause, or unless owing to a changer,
11.348: that implies one of these two, either it is through some cause, or there exists some other being with him as a changer of his will. 349 If they always proceed not through the will of the sacred being,
11.350: from that it is evident that the sacred being is suffering in his own will, and his will is not perfect,
11.351: or there exists some diminisher of it who is a possessor of will.
11.352: As to this, too, which they assert, that the sacred being commanded Adam thus: 'Thou shalt not eat of this one tree which is in paradise (vahist),'
11.354: thus: 'Was the command which the sacred being gave to Adam, thus: "You shall not eat of this tree," good or evil?'
11.355: If the command were good it is evident that the tree was evil;
11.356: and it is not befitting the sacred being to create anything that is evil.
11.357: If the tree were good the command was evil, and it is not befitting the sacred being to give an evil command.
11.358: If the tree were good, and the command as to not eating were given by him, it is not adapted to the goodness and mercifulness of the sacred being to allot a benefit away from his own innocent servants.
11.359: As to this, too, which they assert, that the sacred being brings every one whom he wills unto faith and the true way, and, as the recompense, he makes him proceed to the happy progress which is eternal;
11.360: and him whom he does not will he leaves in irreligion and ignorance of the sacred being, and, for that reason, he casts him into hell and eternal misery;
11.362: thus: 'Is he good whose desire and will are for the religion and faith of the sacred being and the true way, or he whose desire and will are for going astray, irreligion, and ignorance of the sacred being?'
11.363: If one says that he is good whose desire and will are for the religion of the sacred being and the true way,
11.364: now as to that man about whom this is the will of the sacred being, that he shall leave him in irreligion, going astray, and ignorance of the sacred being, and to whom an apostle, or some other person who is a friend, recites the revelation (dînô) of the sacred being and the true way,
11.365: does that show that the sacred being is thereby better and more beneficial to him, or are that apostle and that person so?
11.366: If one says that the will of the sacred being about him is good, it is thereby asserted by him, that not understanding the sacred being, not accepting the religion, and going astray are good; but this is not acceptable [and not to be taught ], on account of error.
11.367: If one says that his coming to the true religion and understanding the sacred being are thereby better and more beneficial,
11.368: it is thereby obviously asserted by one that the apostle and person are thereby better to him than the sacred being.
11.369: Because a person through whom the true way and an understanding of the sacred being are wanted among mankind, and his will is bent upon it, is much better than he who is a sacred being
11.370: by whose will backsliding (avâzrâsîh), misunderstanding, and irreligion exist among them; and the sacred being is much worse than that person.
11.371: Observe this, too, that if the criminal thought and criminal action of man are by the will of the sacred being, that already implies that the sacred being produced criminal thought, and sowed crime in his mind,
11.372: and Aharman merely invites and instigates him to the committal of crime; that shows that the criminal thought traced to the sacred being and also his desire for it are more violent and worse than the invitation of Aharman.
11.373: When, too, his listening to what proceeds from Aharman, as to the committal of crime, is likewise due to the criminal thought which the sacred being produced, and so also is his desire for it, it is already obvious that the sacred being is much worse and more sinful than Aharman.
11.374: As regards these statements, which are enumerated by us,
11.375: one of these two opinions must arise,
11.376: either that all are true or that all are false,
11.377: or there are some which are true and there are some which are false.
11.378: If all be true, every statement that is not adapted to these statements is false, or something of the two, truth and falsehood.
11.379: If all be false, every statement that is not adapted to these statements is true, or something of the two together.
11.380: If there be some that are true and there be some that are false,
11.381: then of those which are true—derived from the nature and nucleus (nâf) of truth—
11.382: and of those which are false—derived from the nature and nucleus and original evolution of falsehood—
11.383: the origins are two, one from which arises truth, and one from which arises falsehood.

12.1: Again, about the inconsistency of their assertions there are several statements from the Dînkard manuscript,
12.2: as to that which they say, that the sacred being is around everything, but nothing is within him;
12.3: and within everything, but nothing is around him.
12.4: That he is above everything, but nothing is below him;
12.5: and below everything, but nothing is above him.
12.6: That he sits upon a throne, but is possessing no resting-place;
12.7: and is inside heaven, but is possessing no whereabouts.
12.8: That he does not exist in any place, and yet he does exist there.
12.9: That he exists everywhere, and yet his place does not exist.
12.10: Also that everything of his becomes fit for his own by his own will,
12.11: his original evolution being both malice and good;
12.12: and he is eternally unforgiving and compassionate,
12.14: Likewise that he has commanded him who is incapable of performing or neglecting the divine command,
12.15: and he has created him who is innocent for hell, not the distresser.
12.16: That he is aware of the hellish existence of mankind, owing to wickedness, and his will is for it;
12.17: and he is good-willed, or it has become not his will.
12.18: That he has produced a remedy, and is not himself distressing;
12.19: or no remedy, but want of remedy, is produced by him, and yet he is not possessing an opponent.
12.20: That he is wanting experience, and yet omniscient;
12.21: neglecting commands, and yet they are themselves his will;
12.22: and he who neglects, and provides a restricted evolution, is yet a good sovereign.
12.23: Also that his commands are all continuous,
12.24: and yet the setting aside of his commands is obtainable.
12.25: And that there is some of his will which is not continuous,
12.26: and neglect of his will is not an injurer of the will.
12.27: Likewise that he has commanded that which is not his will,
12.28: and the command which is not inconsistent with his will and also the command which is inconsistent with his will are both proper.
12.29: Also that his good will is not a discontinuous will,
12.30: and as to his evil will, which makes evil things, that is judicious.
12.31: And many other inconsistencies which are in the assertions of various sects.
12.32: If it be not possible for an orderly (padmânîk) religion to exist, without rescue from these inconsistent assertions of many kinds,
12.33: they then say this of it, that to the supposers of two original evolutions the work of the sacred being is weak and unresisting;
12.34: and they say it is not as it were adapted to the grandeur of the sacred being.
12.35: Upon this subject, too, there are some matters, which I shall clearly state, that should be dictated and known.
12.36: That is, does he make divine things weaker and more unresisting,
12.37: where it is he who says that the sacred being's own achievements, which were created by him, have all lapsed into being intolerant of command and deaf to admonition,
12.38: till even the most tender-bodied creatures struggle against his will?
12.39: And so they have slain or impaled those many prophets (vakhshvarân) and apostles (pêtkhambarân) of his, who are appointed by him;
12.40: and there are some who have acted scornfully, contemptibly, and irreverently.
12.41: This, too, is where he has not only not protected his own dominion from the vile creatures which were created by him himself, but he has himself afflicted his own dominion also;
12.42: and he himself destroys his own productions without a reason,
12.43: and himself renders his own creations useless.
12.44: Through his own culpability he himself destroys his own innocent servants.
12.45: He himself makes his own peculiar friends weak, needy, sinful, and deluded.
12.46: And his wrath, inflicted upon a single innocent servant, which is like Aharman's, makes his own innumerable creatures unobservant and deluded.
12.47: For a sin that is limited, which is owing to his own actions, he puts the innocent to unlimited punishment.
12.48: The door of forgiveness is finally shut up,
12.49: and he is not satiated with the pain, distress, and misery of his own creatures,
12.50: but maintains them perpetually in action and excitement.
12.51: And yet he is not able to insist upon the commands which he gives in the beginning, middle, or end.
12.52: Or is it he who says that that one is the sacred being who is perpetually a ruler, all-knowing and almighty;
12.53: whose dominion and knowledge and power are perpetual and for unlimited time?
12.54: Owing to him, too, is the happiness of any goodness;
12.55: his actions also are for a purpose, his commands are advantageous,
12.56: he is compassionate and forgiving as regards his own servants,
12.57: and is an abundant bestower of recompense, too, on that servant who is a carrier off of victory.
12.58: As to him who is a sinner, who, on account of his own sinfulness, becomes captive in the hands of the enemy, he is forgiving upon atonement for the sinfulness and cleansing from iniquity and pollution.
12.59: In the end he is no leaver of any good creature captive in the hands of enemies,
12.60: and is heir protector, maintainer, and cherisher, in body and life, amid their contest and struggle with enemies.
12.61: He is a complete defender of his own empire from opponents of a different nature,
12.62: and his champions and troops become victorious in the struggle and contest.
12.63: And in the end he is a bringer of victory to his own creatures, as regards every iniquity.
12.64: When it is observed as to light, knowledge, sight, life, health, and other divine creations, that they are fully resistant and prevailing over darkness, ignorance, blindness, death, sickness, and other demoniacal peculiarities—
12.65: because this is known, that light is the putting aside of all darkness,
12.67: and life is powerful and increasing over death,
12.68: for, owing to the powerfulness and increase of life, the incalculable progress of the creatures arises from two persons,
12.69: and multitudes are confident about it;
12.70: so also sight and health are manifestly as much victorious and powerful over blindness and sickness —
12.71: such being observed, it is also expedient to observe this, that is, what does the opposing fiend want, and about what do the troops of the sacred being struggle?
12.72: That opponent wants this that he speaks of thus: 'I will make this earth and sky and the creatures which are luminaries extinct,
12.73: or I will bring them into my possession, and will pervert them from their own nature,
12.74: so that the sacred being shall not be able to occasion the resurrection and the renovation of the universe, and to restore his own creatures.'
12.75: The troops of the sacred being struggle about this, that the opponent shall not attain to his will through his desire.
12.76: Observe this, too, that the troops of Aûharmazd have been valiant in struggling and successful in will ever since the original creation.
12.77: From this it is manifest, when it happens that this earth and sky are formed,
12.78: that it would be possible for him to make all creatures and creations extinct; but he is incapable of making even one of the most tender-bodied creatures of the sacred being extinct.
12.79: Because, if even, by reason of death, the body be separated from life, it is not extinction and change of nature from its own self, but decay of peculiarities and a necessity of going from place to place, from duty to duty.
12.80: Then each one of the qualities of one's body and life is to subsist again, in its own nature, for other duties, as is revealed.
12.81: And the existence of these creatures and creation, fully continuously and perpetually active, is advantageously manifest during a suitable period.
12.82: Thus far is considered complete upon this subject.

13.1: Again, about the inconsistency and faulty statements of the first scripture,
13.3: and as to it they are, in every way, unanimous that the sacred being wrote it with his own hand, and gave it to Moses (Mûshâê)—
13.4: so that, as it is full of delusion, I will here publish, for your information, a story out of all its stupidity and of much that is in it.
13.5: It states, in the beginning of the scripture,
13.6: that there first arose earth, without form and void, darkness, and black water;
13.7: and the breathing of the sacred being ever yearns over the face of that black water.
13.8: Afterwards the sacred being spoke thus: 'Let there be light,'
13.10: And stooping he considered that light below him,
13.11: and the light was transmitted by him to the day, and the darkness to the night.
13.12: In six days this world and sky and earth were also created by him,
13.13: for during the seventh day he was reposing (khaspân) and comfortable.
13.14: Through that same mystery (râz) even now the Jews are enjoying repose on the Sabbath day.
13.15: This, too, is stated, that Adam and his wife Eve (Havâê) were created by him,
13.16: and put into a garden of paradise (vahist);
13.17: so that Adam should perform cultivation in that garden, and should keep watch.
13.18: The Lord, who is the sacred being himself, commanded Adam
13.19: thus: 'Eat of every tree which is in this garden, except of that tree of knowledge;
13.20: because when you eat thereof you die.'
13.21: Afterwards a serpent was also put by him into the garden;
13.22: and that serpent deceived Eve and spoke thus: 'Let us eat of the gathering from this tree, and let us give it to Adam.'
13.25: And his knowledge became such that good was distinguished by him from evil, and they did not die.
13.26: He also saw and knew that he was naked,
13.27: and became concealed under the trees;
13.28: he likewise covered over his own body with leaves of trees, on account of the shame of nakedness.
13.29: Afterwards the Lord went to the garden, and called Adam by name thus: 'Where art thou?'
13.30: Adam replied thus: 'Here I am, under the trees, for this reason, because I am naked.'
13.32: and spoke thus: 'Who could have informed thee that thou art naked?
13.33: Mayest thou not ever yet have eaten of that tree of knowledge, of which I said that you shall not eat?'
13.34: Adam spoke thus: 'I have been deceived by this woman, who was given to me by thee, and I ate.'
13.35: And the Lord enquired of Eve thus: 'Why was it so done by thee?'
13.36: Eve spoke thus: 'I have been deceived by this serpent.'
13.37: And Adam and Eve and the serpent are, all three, forced out of the garden of paradise by him with a curse.
13.38: And he spoke to Adam thus: 'Thy eating shall be through the scraping off of sweat and the panting of the nostrils,
13.39: until the end of thy life;
13.40: and thy land shall grow all bodily refuse and dung.'
13.41: He also spoke to Eve thus: 'Thy pregnancy shall be in pain and uneasy, and thy bringing forth in grievous hastening.'
13.42: And he spoke to the serpent thus: 'Thou shalt be accursed from amid the quadrupeds and wild animals of the plain and mountain;
13.43: for thee also there shall be no feet,
13.44: and thy movement shall be on thy belly, and thy food dust.
13.45: And betwixt thy offspring, with those of the woman, there shall be such hatred and conversion to enmity that they will wound the head of that offspring.'
13.46: This, too, they say, that this worldly existence, with whatever is in everything, was made and produced by him for mankind;
13.47: and man was made by him predominant over all creatures and creations, wet and dry.
13.48: Now I will tell you a story (nisang-1) about the contents of their twaddle and the faultiness of their statements,
13.49: that is, where and with what limits did that earth without form and void, the darkness, the sacred being and his breathing, and the black water arise?
13.50: Or of what description was the sacred being himself?
13.51: It is manifest that he was not light,
13.52: because, when the light was seen by him,
13.53: stooping he considered it, for the reason that he had not seen it before.
13.54: If they say that he was dark, that manifestly implies that the origin of darkness is uttering a word and there is light.
13.55: If they say that he was not dark, but light,
13.56: why, when the light was seen by him, did he admire and consider it, though he was light himself?
13.57: And if they say that he was neither light nor dark,
13.58: it is necessary for such to specify that third state which is not light and not dark.
13.59: Then as to him whose position and abode were in darkness and black water, and light was never seen by him, how was it possible for him to look at that light?
13.60: And what was his divinity owing to?
13.61: Because even now it is not possible for any one who remains in darkness to look at the light.
13.62: Observe also this, that if his origin and abode were darkness, how was it possible for him to remain opposite the light?
13.63: Because this is known, that it is not possible for darkness to remain opposite the light, since the latter puts it aside harmless.
13.64: Again, I ask this, that is, was that earth, which was without form and void, limited or unlimited?
13.65: If it were limited, what was there outside of it?
13.66: If it were unlimited, whither did that unlimitedness of it go,
13.67: when, as we see, this earth and worldly existence are not those of the first existence?
13.68: As to that which the Lord spoke,
13.69: that is: 'Let there be light,' and it was so,
13.70: it is thereupon appropriate to understand that the Lord existed before the time that the light arose;
13.71: and when he was wishing to make the light, and he gave the command for it to arise, he then considered mentally in what way the light is of good appearance or evil appearance.
13.72: And if the light, through its own nature, reached into the knowledge and consideration of the Lord, it is evident that the light was existing alike within the knowledge and mind of the Lord,
13.74: For it is not possible to know and obtain anything, unless it be a manifestation of an existence.
13.75: If the light was existing is it, on that account, a creation of the Lord?
13.76: And if they say that the light was not, through its own nature, within his knowledge, that light was demanded by him, who did not know of what nature it was, very unwisely.
13.77: Or how is it possible to consider in the mind that which one has never even thought of or known?
13.78: And observe this, too, that that command for the arising of light was given either to something or to nothing,
13.79: because this is certain, that it is necessary to give a command to a performer of commands.
13.80: If it were given by him to something existing, which was light, that implies that the light itself existed.
